The stated uncertainties for wind speed and wind direction may be sufficient for the relative comparison to detect underperformance between turbines, but they do not meet the requirements for an absolute performance validation according to IEC 61400-12-1 (2005) or IEC 61400-12-2 (2013). One could perform power curve verification tests in accordance with the mentioned standards at turbines where they are applicable, and those turbines that are reference turbines in the monitoring method would increase the confidence in underperformance detection. At least for the concurrent period.

Title: A SCADA-Informed Framework Combining Machine Learning and Wind Speed Correction for Yaw Misalignment Detection
Snippet: This study presented a SCADA-only framework for detecting static yaw misalignment in operating wind turbines. The approach embeds a parametric yaw loss function into a Gaussian Process power curve model, enabling direct estimation of static yaw offsets from trained model parameters while explicitly accounting for observation uncertainty. A consensus-based wind speed correction step is incorporated to mitigate yaw-dependent biases in nacelle anemometer measurements. Application to the Kelmarsh wind farm yields offset estimates consistent in sign and magnitude across turbines and AEP losses in line with literature values, demonstrating the potential of the framework for scalable, data-driven yaw misalignment detection. Ongoing and future work, as discussed above, focuses on external validation, relaxing the symmetry assumption of the loss function, and developing uncertainty-aware estimates of the inferred yaw offsets.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: Deviation of drive torque and rotational speed of a wind turbine drivetrain between test bench and wind turbine simulations
Snippet: The correct representation of the loads acting at the hub and throughout the drivetrain tested at system test benches is important as these are used to validate the wind turbine simulation models and to predict the drivetrain's behaviour of the erected wind turbine. The differences between erected wind turbine (wind turbine with rotor and tower) and test bench (nacelle with drive unit and wind load unit) lead to deviations in hub loads. This paper focusses on the deviations of the hub torque and rotational speed between erected wind turbine and bench tests using simulation models. Hub torque and rotational speed values are generally represented well by the test bench drive unit. The torque time series values of the field application are maximum 5 % higher than at the test bench for low wind speeds and maximum 2 % higher compared to the rated torque. The deviations can result from the way the torque is applied at the test bench as the drive unit sets the rotational speed and the DUT sets the corresponding torque: The drivetrain efficiency of the aerodynamic simulation is lower than the test bench drivetrain efficiency as the drivetrain efficiency in the aerodynamic simulation also includes losses from e.g. the pitch drives, the converter etc. Thus, the aerodynamic torque must be higher to reach the same generator torque. Another reason is the different inertias of the drivetrains of the erected wind turbine and the test bench. This lower torque at the test bench leads to an underestimation of the acting component loads and displacements in the drivetrain at the test bench relative to the erected wind turbine and thus needs to be investigated in the future for the gearbox components. 

Future work will also compare the accuracy of the representation of thrust, lateral forces and bending moments as these are the relevant loads for the main bearings. Further work will focus also on the deviations in the drivetrain response to the acting loads evaluating accelerations, displacements and loads in the drivetrain using MBS and FEM. Finally, the goal is to identify the reasons for the deviations IOP Publishing doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2767/4/042013 10 which may lie in the load application system or the stiffness of the connections to the test bench. The following step will be the investigation of design adjustments of the test bench to reduce these deviations.
</snippet>

Title: Wind turbine drivetrains: state-of-the-art technologies and future development trends
Snippet: Abstract. This paper presents the state-of-the-art technologies and development trends of wind turbine drivetrains – the energy conversion systems transferring the kinetic energy of the wind to electrical energy – in different stages of their life cycle: design, manufacturing, installation, operation, lifetime extension, decommissioning, and recycling. Offshore development and digitalization are also a focal point in this study. The main aim of this article is to review the drivetrain technology development as well as to identify future challenges and research gaps. Drivetrain in this context includes the whole power conversion system: main bearing, shafts, gearbox, generator, and power converter. The paper discusses current design technologies for each component along with advantages and disadvantages. The discussion of the operation phase highlights the condition monitoring methods currently employed by the industry as well as emerging areas. This article also illustrates the multidisciplinary aspect of wind turbine drivetrains, which emphasizes the need for more interdisciplinary research and collaboration.
</snippet>

Title: Monitoring Wind Turbine Loading Using Power Converter Signals
Snippet: The ability to detect faults and predict loads on a wind turbine drivetrain's mechanical components cost-effectively is critical to making the cost of wind energy competitive. In order to investigate whether this is possible using the readily available power converter current signals, an existing permanent magnet synchronous generator based wind energy conversion system computer model was modified to include a grid-side converter (GSC) for an improved converter model and a gearbox. The GSC maintains a constant DC link voltage via vector control. The gearbox was modelled as a 3-mass model to allow faults to be included. Gusts and gearbox faults were introduced to investigate the ability of the machine side converter (MSC) current (Iq) to detect and quantify loads on the mechanical components. In this model, gearbox faults were not detectable in the Iq signal due to shaft stiffness and damping interaction. However, a model that predicts the load change on mechanical wind turbine components using Iq was developed and verified using synthetic and real wind data.
</snippet>

Title: Field validation of dynamic mechanical torque measurements using fiber-optic strain sensors for geared wind turbines
Snippet: Wind turbine power ratings, rotor diameters, and hub heights have grown significantly to reduce the cost of wind energy [1]. The wind turbine drivetrain converts mechanical power to electrical power and transmits the rotor loads to the bedplate and tower [2]; it makes an appreciable contribution to the capital expenditure of the turbine [3]. Many wind turbine drivetrains use gearboxes to lower the capital cost of the drivetrain, but its reliability is essential and remains a top priority because gearbox failures cause long downtime with costly repairs and contribute appreciably to the turbine operation and maintenance costs [4][5][6]. Thanks to internationally recognized gearbox wind turbine design standards like IEC 61400-4 and AGMA 6006 and collaborative efforts like the Drivetrain Reliability Collaborative between turbine manufacturers, gearbox designers, bearing suppliers, and research institutions like the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and Argonne National Laboratory, average annual gearbox failure rates for the U.S. land-based fleet have dropped from 5% to 10% 20 years ago [7] to 2.5% more recently [8]. Yet, there is room for improvement because gearboxes still generally do not reach their desired design life [9]. These standards have placed greater rigor on the design and gearbox verification process, including the effects of rotor nontorque loads [10], transient events [11,12], and electrical currents [13]. However, the rapid pace at which torque density requirements have risen has led to increasingly complex and lightweight designs with new reliability challenges and additional requirements, such as complying with stricter noise demands and more prominent dynamic interactions. 

Accurate knowledge of the dynamic mechanical torque in wind turbine gearboxes is essential to complying with these requirements and improving their reliability. Dynamic mechanical torque measurements of every gearbox in a fleet can enhance drivetrain usage monitoring because the consumed fatigue life can be assessed more precisely using the measured torque values throughout their entire commercial operation. Dynamic torque measurements can also potentially be used by the wind turbine controller for improved wind turbine control to achieve a reduction of torque oscillations (i.e., torsional damping). Additionally, dynamic mechanical torque measurements can be used to quantify drivetrain efficiency.
</snippet>

Title: Influence of drivetrain efficiency determination on the torque control of wind turbines
Snippet: Decreasing the levelized cost of energy is a major design objective for wind turbines. Accordingly, the control is generally optimized to achieve a high energy production and a high-power coefficient. In partial load range, speed and torque are controlled via the generator torque but the rotor torque determines the power coefficient of the turbine. High uncertainties for the uncalibrated low-speed shaft torque measurement and varying drivetrain efficiencies which depend on the speed, load and temperature lead to a torque control error that reduces the power coefficient of the wind turbine. In this paper the rotor torque control error and the impact on the power coefficient of wind turbines is quantified. For this purpose, the variation of drivetrain efficiency is analyzed. An efficiency model for the wind turbine drivetrain is build and validated on the test bench. Then, the influence of the drivetrain speed, torque loads, non-torque loads, and temperature on the efficiency is quantified. Finally, the influence of the rotor torque control error on the power coefficient was simulated with an aerodynamic model. The results show that of all examined influences only torque and temperature significantly impacting the efficiency leading to rotor torque control errors that reduce the power coefficient and consequently increase the levelized cost of energy. Improved efficiency measurement on WT test benches or drivetrain efficiency modelling can reduce the rotor torque control error and therefore decrease the LCOE. Summary
Across 2020–2025 wind turbine conversion efficiency studies, several performance metrics are repeatedly unreported or underweighted despite being critical to quantify real-world energy conversion and cost. These include drivetrain and power-electronics losses, partial-load/temperature-dependent efficiency, alignment and environmental losses (yaw, icing, turbulence/wakes), measurement uncertainty and site-specific recalibration of power curves, and system-level economic indicators (AEP, capacity factor, LCOE, and energy payback). Omitting these metrics biases comparisons, misstates design trade-offs, and obscures risks to reliability and profitability. <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1 defines the accepted power performance assessment framework (instrumentation, meteorological mast, air density, control state), yet many studies do not propagate these uncertainties or report them</cite> <cite id="e9ac28bc-2">and the uncertainties tolerated for monitoring differ from those required for absolute validation, which can mask underperformance</cite>. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Moreover, unmodeled drivetrain and temperature effects can erode rotor torque control and reduce the power coefficient, increasing LCOE</cite>. Below, we detail the absent metrics and why they matter.

I. What “conversion efficiency” means and what gets measured
Conversion efficiency in wind energy typically decomposes into aerodynamic capture (often the rotor power coefficient Cp), drivetrain/mechanical transmission efficiency, and electrical conversion/conditioning efficiency to grid-tied output. <cite id="b277c7c4-0">The system efficiency includes blade aerodynamics, gearbox, and generator efficiencies</cite> <cite id="b277c7c4-2">and Betz’s 59.3% upper bound applies to ideal rotor capture, with real losses from flow deflection, pressure recovery, and mechanical/electrical pathways</cite>. In practice, many studies report Cp or power curves without explicitly separating mechanical and electrical losses or contextualizing them with operating conditions and site-specific wind. <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1 specifies measurement of power versus wind speed, air density, wind direction, control state, and instrumentation calibration, but studies often omit uncertainty budgets and site-specific validation</cite>.

II. Metrics systematically absent or underreported
1) Drivetrain and converter (conditioning) losses
- Absence: Many conversion-efficiency papers treat the rotor-to-shaft-to-generator path as a single “efficiency” or focus on Cp, with little quantification of gearbox, bearing, and converter losses as functions of speed, torque, temperature, and load regime. <cite id="59cd79f3-0">Comparisons between bench and field show that drivetrain efficiency in aerodynamic simulations is lower than test-bench efficiencies when losses from pitch drives and the converter are included, implying that neglecting these components underestimates required aerodynamic torque and overstates net conversion</cite>. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Variations in drivetrain efficiency with speed, load, and temperature, and uncalibrated low-speed shaft torque measurements, create rotor torque control errors that reduce Cp and raise LCOE</cite>. 
- Why it matters: Drivetrain and converter losses are not passive; they change with operating point and temperature, altering optimal control and energy yield. <cite id="59cd79f3-3">Gearbox reliability and cost dominate O&M; accurate torque and efficiency monitoring enable better control for torsional damping and efficiency</cite>. Omitting these losses leads to overoptimistic energy capture and underestimates downtime and maintenance impacts.

2) Partial-load and temperature-dependent efficiency
- Absence: Studies frequently emphasize rated Cp and power curve slope while downplaying partial-load efficiency and temperature corrections, even though most operating hours fall below rated and temperature affects air density, viscosity, and lubrication losses. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">In partial load, generator torque controls speed while rotor torque sets Cp; uncertainties in low-speed shaft torque and variable drivetrain efficiency (speed, load, temperature) produce torque-control errors that reduce Cp and increase LCOE</cite>. 
- Why it matters: Without separating partial-load efficiency and temperature effects, “conversion efficiency” averages can misrepresent energy capture during the dominant operating regime and hide control penalties that inflate LCOE. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Improved drivetrain efficiency modeling or test-bench measurement can reduce rotor torque control error and lower LCOE</cite>.

3) Alignment and environmental losses (yaw, icing, turbulence/wakes)
- Absence: Yaw misalignment, icing, and wake interactions are often treated as rare events or qualitative concerns rather than quantified efficiency losses in conversion studies. <cite id="e9ac28bc-1">IEC-aligned instrumentation and yaw-offset campaigns demonstrate that misalignment measurably affects loads and power, but many conversion studies do not report yaw-loss metrics</cite> <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">and SCADA-informed frameworks quantify static yaw offsets and associated AEP losses consistent with literature</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-2">In wind-farm layout optimization, conversion efficiency is measured relative to an ideal power ϑr(v) unaffected by wakes, yet many case studies do not report wake-induced efficiency penalties in routine performance reporting</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-0">In cold climates, icing reduces performance and causes power losses; climatic ice accretion also increases fatigue loads</cite>.
- Why it matters: Unmeasured yaw and wake losses can amount to several percent AEP loss per turbine and propagate across farms; icing losses degrade both energy yield and structural health. <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">AEP loss estimates from SCADA-based yaw detection align with literature values, underscoring that static yaw alone can materially reduce lifetime energy</cite>.

4) Measurement uncertainty, site-specific recalibration, and absolute validation
- Absence: Several studies adopt manufacturer power curves without site recalibration or publish detailed uncertainty budgets, despite standards guidance. <cite id="e9ac28bc-3">Manufacturers provide power curves per IEC 61400-12-1, but differences between expected and in-situ generation motivate post-installation power curve recalibration; using manufacturer curves without change can misstate performance</cite>. <cite id="e9ac28bc-2">Uncertainties acceptable for relative turbine comparisons do not meet the requirements for absolute performance validation per IEC 61400-12-1/12-2; nevertheless, many monitoring approaches rely on these weaker uncertainty bounds</cite>. 
- Why it matters: <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1 mandates comprehensive instrumentation (wind speed/direction, air density, power, control state) and site calibration; omitting these steps or uncertainty propagation can delay detection of underperformance and inflate efficiency estimates</cite>.

5) System-level economic and energy-balance metrics
- Absence: Conversion efficiency papers often stop at Cp or percent of Betz, without linking to AEP, capacity factor, LCOE, or energy payback. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Because rotor torque control errors reduce Cp, the same efficiency shortfall translates directly into increased LCOE</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-0">System-level analyses estimate efficiency trends and then project cost trajectories (Moore’s Law analogy) under constant efficiency assumptions, highlighting the need to connect efficiency to costs and lifetimes</cite>. 
- Why it matters: <cite id="59cd79f3-4">A reduction in power coefficient increases LCOE even when Cp is nominally “high,” so studies that optimize Cp without tracking LCOE misalign efficiency gains with economic value</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-0">Assuming constant efficiency over time can understate or overstate lifetime energy and costs when real efficiency drifts with O&M, maintenance, or component degradation</cite>.

III. Why the omission matters: mechanisms and magnitudes
- Control and optimization loops: <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Modern control optimizes Cp and energy production, but if drivetrain efficiency varies with speed/torque/temperature, the controller’s assumptions are invalid and rotor torque errors reduce Cp; quantifying drivetrain efficiency and temperature effects reduces these errors and LCOE</cite>. <cite id="59cd79f3-3">Accurate dynamic mechanical torque measurement enables better usage monitoring, torsional damping, and efficiency quantification for gearboxes, which are primary O&M hotspots</cite>.
- Measurement and reporting integrity: <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1 defines the rigorous test and measurement procedure; many studies do not publish site calibration details or uncertainty budgets, which are essential to compare across machines and sites</cite> <cite id="e9ac28bc-2">and the tolerance for relative comparisons is not sufficient for absolute validation, risking undetected underperformance</cite>. <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">SCADA frameworks that embed yaw-loss functions and wind-speed corrections can recover AEP losses consistent with literature, indicating that static yaw alone often causes nontrivial lifetime energy deficits</cite>.
- Environmental and operational losses: <cite id="e9ac28bc-1">Yaw-offset field campaigns show direct links between misalignment, loads, and power; without reporting yaw-loss metrics, conversion efficiency appears artificially high</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-2">Wake-aware optimization defines an “ideal” power ϑr(v) unaffected by wakes; neglecting wake-induced reductions in routine studies overestimates achievable conversion efficiency in farms</cite>. <cite id="13ee5899-0">Icing events reduce output and increase fatigue, yet many studies do not quantify ice-induced efficiency loss or its frequency</cite>.
- Economic implications: <cite id="59cd79f3-4">For a given Cp reduction, LCOE rises proportionally, so omitting LCOE linkages obscures the true value impact of conversion inefficiencies</cite>. <cite id="59cd79f3-3">Gearbox failures cause long downtime and costly repairs; accurate torque/efficiency monitoring is essential to maintain reliability and avoid hidden energy penalties</cite>.
- Standards and replicability: <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1/-12-2 delineate procedures and required measurements (power, wind speed/direction, air density, control state, pitch/rotational speed), yet many studies omit key parameters or do not disclose procedures, impeding replication and comparison</cite>. <cite id="e9ac28bc-1">Load and power instrumentation must be time-synchronous and conform to IEC 61409-2; inconsistent or missing metadata reduces interpretability of “efficiency” results</cite>.

IV. What to report instead: a checklist for conversion-efficiency studies (2020–2025)
- Decompose efficiency: Report Cp (rotor power coefficient), drivetrain efficiency (mechanical transmission), and converter/electrical conditioning efficiency, ideally as functions of wind speed, torque, temperature, and load regime. <cite id="b277c7c4-0">System efficiency includes blades, gearbox, and generator</cite> <cite id="59cd79f3-0">and including pitch drive and converter losses changes benchmarking</cite>.
- Partial-load and temperature: Provide partial-load Cp maps and temperature-corrected air-density curves; quantify torque-control error margins and their effect on Cp and LCOE. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Low-speed shaft torque uncertainty and drivetrain efficiency variation drive rotor torque control errors that reduce Cp and increase LCOE</cite>.
- Alignment and environment: Include yaw misalignment indices and associated AEP loss budgets; quantify icing loss frequency and magnitude where applicable; account for wake interference in farm-level evaluations. <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">SCADA-informed yaw misalignment detection yields AEP-consistent loss estimates</cite> <cite id="13ee5899-2">and wake-aware conversion metrics avoid overestimating farm efficiency</cite>.
- Measurement integrity: Publish IEC 61400-12-1/-12-2 compliant procedures, site calibration metadata, and uncertainty budgets; distinguish relative monitoring uncertainties from absolute validation requirements. <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC procedures mandate meteorological mast, air density, control state, and instrument calibration</cite> <cite id="e9ac28bc-2">and absolute validation requires stricter uncertainty control than many monitoring studies</cite>.
- System-level linkage: Tie conversion efficiency to AEP, capacity factor, and LCOE; show sensitivity of LCOE to Cp and drivetrain/temperature-driven control errors; include energy payback considerations over lifetime. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Cp reductions directly increase LCOE; improved drivetrain efficiency modeling reduces control errors and lowers LCOE</cite> <cite id="13ee5899-0">and treating efficiency as time-invariant can misstate lifetime energy and costs</cite>.
- Drivetrain and gearbox: Report dynamic torque measurement methods (e.g., fiber-optic strain sensors) and use them for usage monitoring, torsional damping, and efficiency quantification; connect to O&M risk. <cite id="59cd79f3-3">Dynamic torque measurement enhances drivetrain usage monitoring and can quantify drivetrain efficiency</cite>.

V. Domain-specific considerations and remaining gaps
- Urban and complex terrain: <cite id="13ee5899-0">Studies often assume constant efficiency across commissioning years, but urban growth, turbulence, and siting changes alter in-situ performance, warranting time-varying efficiency modeling and recalibration</cite>.
- Farm-level optimization: <cite id="13ee5899-2">Conversion efficiency metrics that ignore wake effects can overstate achievable output; farm studies should report wake-induced efficiency penalties and layout sensitivity</cite>.
- Small and vertical-axis turbines: <cite id="b277c7c4-1">Betz limit provides a benchmark, but practical power coefficients are typically lower and vary with tip-speed ratio; many small turbine studies emphasize aerodynamic design without quantifying drivetrain/converter losses or control-dependent partial-load efficiency</cite>.
- Standards alignment: <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1/-12-2 provide robust procedures; however, the proprietary nature of some verification methods and incomplete disclosure limit cross-study comparability</cite>. <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">Open SCADA frameworks that embed loss functions can improve transparency and detection of underperformance</cite>.

Conclusion
Recent conversion-efficiency studies frequently omit drivetrain and converter loss profiles, partial-load and temperature dependence, alignment/environmental losses, rigorous uncertainty budgets, and economic linkages (AEP/LCOE/energy payback). These omissions matter because they invalidate controller and design optimizations, mask real energy shortfalls, and misattribute economic performance. <cite id="59cd79f3-4">Even small errors in drivetrain efficiency and torque control can reduce Cp and raise LCOE</cite>, while <cite id="e9ac28bc-2">relaxing uncertainty standards can let underperformance go undetected</cite>. Adopting IEC-aligned measurement frameworks, decomposing efficiency pathways, and tying metrics to AEP and LCOE improve comparability and decision-usefulness, and better reflect the physics and economics of wind energy conversion. <cite id="e9ac28bc-0">IEC 61400-12-1 provides the backbone for credible reporting</cite> and <cite id="e9ac28bc-4">data-driven detection of yaw and control losses demonstrates the value of including these metrics in modern studies</cite>. </answer>

Snippet: Wind turbine efficiency is the capability of a turbine to convert the kinetic energy of wind into electrical output. According to Betz's law [41], the theoretical maximum efficiency achievable by any wind turbine is 59.3%; however, practical efficiencies remain lower due to aerodynamic and mechanical limitations [42]. 

Given the scarcity of comprehensive historical efficiency data, we estimate wind turbine efficiencies across different commissioning years using other technical specifications compiled from [43]. These specifications include key parameters such as rotor diameter, rated power, rated wind speed, cut-in and cut-out wind speeds, and commissioning year. The power curve approximation function available in the NREL SAM [33] is used to derive the efficiency of each turbine. Analysis of the calculated efficiencies, plotted against commissioning years (Figure 3b), revealed no discernible temporal trend. This result led us to assume a constant wind turbine efficiency over time, in line with the literature [42,44]. 

Following the efficiency assessment, technological advancement is quantified through the analysis of installation cost trends. Historical global weighted-average installed cost data for onshore wind power plants [45] are presented in Figure 3a (left) as solid circles, alongside an exponential trend line projecting future expenditures. This decline, analogous to Moore's Law, provides a deterministic technological advancement trajectory under the assumption of constant turbine efficiency. An exponential fit to cost data from 2009 to 2022 yields an annual cost multiplier of 0.9599, corresponding to a five-year multiplier of 0.8149. Installation costs for wind projects are influenced by turbine specifications, hub heights, and administrative and logistical requirements. For the case study, a representative project scheduled for 2024 was selected. Located approximately 222.5 kilometers from the METU campus, it consists of four Goldwind GW165-6.0 turbines-the sole candidate model considered-providing a total capacity of 24 MW with an expected operational lifetime of 25 years. 

Historical O&M cost data, sourced from [46] and normalized by installed capacity, are shown in Figure 3a (solid diamonds). These costs are extrapolated using an exponential trend to forecast future O&M expenditures.

From continents spanning the globe to remote island nations, the potential for wind energy is vast, providing a pathway toward a cleaner and more sustainable future. Through this methodical approach, the review provides a comprehensive overview of current research in wind turbine efficiency, aiding decision-makers in the field. snippet.text: Exploring the enhancement of wind turbine efficiency reveals the possibility of a wide array of innovations and challenges across different regions. From continents spanning the globe to remote island nations, the potential for wind energy is vast, providing a pathway toward a cleaner and more sustainable future. Despite facing turbulence in policy, technology, and markets, wind power remains a promising solution. Here, based on our previous studies (Eftekhari et al., 2022;Alawad et al., 2022;Husain et al., 2023;Namasivayam et al., 2023;Khaleel et al., 2024;Shafiq et al., 2024) this systematic literature review conducted using the Scopus database, meticulously curated relevant studies on improvements in wind turbine efficiency. By employing specific search terms and criteria, pertinent studies were selected and evaluated to extract essential insights and methodologies. Through this methodical approach, the review provides a comprehensive overview of current research in wind turbine efficiency, aiding decision-makers in the field. This review also adds suggestions and supports current issues in the sustainable development goals (SDGs), as reported elsewhere (see Table 2).

Title: A Wind Turbine Efficiency Limit Higher than the Lanchester (Betz) Limit
Snippet: The efficiency of a wind turbine system normally includes the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades, the efficiency of the gearbox, if any, and that of the generator. The aerodynamic efficiency referred to in this study is the fraction of power reaching the rotating shaft divided by the total rate at which energy approaches the turbine in the form of wind. This is sometimes called the power coefficient. 

After Hütter (1977) suggested that the well-known wind turbine aerodynamic efficiency limit of 59% was not a definite upper limit, and Inglis (1979) pointed out that at least one wind turbine may have achieved an efficiency higher than this limit, Greet (1980) observed problems in the force balance implied by the historical derivation and stated, consequently, that no such limit could be found in a one-dimensional analysis. Rauh and Seelert (1984) confirmed that no theoretically grounded optimum for the aerodynamic efficiency of windmills existed. 

As van Kuik (2007) pointed out, the limit was first derived by Lanchester (1915) and then by Joukowsky (1920) and Betz (1920Betz ( , 1928)), so it is called the Lanchester-Betz-Joukowsky limit (see also Bergey 1979). However, the work of Betz was the most available to readers, so the name "Betz limit" was used for some years. For further discussion on this topic and some inefficiencies of wind turbines, see Georgiou and Theodoropoulos (2011). To the author's knowledge, no study to date has incorporated an angular momentum analysis to propose an alternate limit.

Title: Mechanical Augmentation Channel Design for Turbine Current Generators
Snippet: For propeller-type turbines efficiency is defined as the ratio between the turbine power and the power of an unconstrained uniform flow through the turbine area. The efficiency limit of Betz (59.3%) is usually considered for this kind of turbines. 

The Betz model considers that the fluid flow remains rectilinear when passing through the turbine and maintains a uniform distribution of the fluid pressure. This consideration overestimates the forces and torque applied to the turbine and overestimates the turbine's power and its efficiency. The case is that the fluid streams experience a deflection from the rectilinear direction, changing their motion to curvilinear trajectories and reducing their pressure on the turbine. It is possible to get a more accurate efficiency limit by taking into account these considerations. 

New models like the GGS model [14] have been proposed. In the Betz model the center of pressure is at a distance /2 from the axis, where  is the turbine radius, whereas in the GGS model the center of pressure is at a distance 0.37 from the turbine axis, much closer to the turbine shaft. Then the torque is greater in the Betz model than in the GGS model as a result of this difference. 

One way to increase the efficiency of these turbines is to install augmentation channels (ACHs) to accelerate flow speed. With regard to this augmentation devices different terms such as duct, shroud, wind-lens, nozzle, concentrator, diffuser, or ACH are used synonymously [15]. Some other reports on channel augmentation can be found in [16][17][18][19]. 

Ducted turbines are not subjected to the Betz limit. For ducted turbines the theoretical limit depends on (a) the pressure difference between duct inlet and outlet and (b) the volumetric flow through the duct. These factors depend on the shape of the duct and the ratio of duct area to turbine area. 

Previous investigations by others [20,21] have found a theoretical limit for a diffuser-augmented wind turbine of about 3.3 times the Betz limit, and a model diffuseraugmented wind turbine has extracted 4.25 times the power extracted by the same turbine without a diffuser.

Snippet: According to [32], the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) has bundled together under the number 61,400 several standards for different sectors of the wind energy. For example, five of these standards are the following: Overall, IEC 61400-12-1 encompasses the procedure for power performance assessment of wind turbines, including measurement instrumentation and data analysis. IEC 61400-12-1:2005 specifies a procedure for measuring the power performance characteristics of a single wind turbine and applies to the testing of wind turbines of all types and sizes connected to the electrical power network. It also describes a procedure to be used to determine the power performance characteristics of small wind turbines when connected to either the electric power network or a battery bank. New versions such as IEC 61400-12-2:2013 specify a procedure for verifying the power performance characteristics of a single electricity-producing, horizontal axis wind turbine, which is not considered to be a small wind turbine per IEC 61400-2. This standard is intended to be used when the specific operational or contractual specifications may not comply with the requirements set forth in IEC 61400-12-1:2005 [1]. 

In accordance with [1], the parameters that are taken into consideration for the assessment of the power curve of the wind turbine are the following: 

In short, the test site is the position of the wind turbine under assessment and its vicinity. Here, a meteorological mast must be installed near the wind turbine to measure wind speed and direction. This process involves an experimental site calibration, which requires the installation of one more meteorological mast, anemometers, wind direction sensors, and a data acquisition system along with a data logger. In addition, equipment is needed for carrying out the following measurements: electric power, wind speed, wind direction, air density, rotational speed and pitch angle, blade condition, and wind turbine control system. 

Furthermore, regarding the measurement procedure, it is a well-known fact that companies that carry out the power performance verification of wind turbines keep the know-how of their measurement procedures as classified information. Therefore, it is not very common to find detailed step-by-step information about this procedure.

Title: Assessment of wind turbine component loads under yaw-offset conditions
Snippet: The field-test campaign was carried out at the NWTC near Boulder, Colorado, and occurred over 6 months, during which the test turbine was operated with discrete yaw offsets over a range of wind speeds and atmospheric conditions. The test turbine and its dedicated meteorological tower are shown in Fig. 1. Details of the turbine are provided in Table 1. 

The turbine was instrumented in accordance with IEC 61400-13 (IEC, 2015) for mechanical-load measurements. All measurement methods and load processing were in conformance with this standard. Specifically, the tower base, tower top, and blade roots were instrumented for measurement of bending loads. In addition, the tower top and main shaft were instrumented for torque measurements. Encoders were used to measure yaw position, blade pitch, and rotor azimuth. The turbine was also instrumented for independent power measurements (per IEC, 2017). All signals were collected with a time-synchronous deterministic EtherCAT protocol and stored at a sample rate of 50 Hz. 

The meteorological tower is located 161 m (∼ 2 rotor diameters) in the predominant upwind direction of the turbine and was instrumented in accordance with IEC 61400-12-1 (IEC, 2017). The meteorological tower measurement signals were time-synchronously recorded with the turbine loads sig-nals. For the analysis presented in this paper, the 80 m cup anemometer and the 87 m wind vane signal were used for the reference mean wind speed, direction, and turbulence intensity (TI). Test data were limited to a sector of directions in which the meteorological tower is largely upwind of the turbine. This measurement sector avoids any turbine wake influence on the meteorological tower instrumentation or influence of other turbines at the test site. More details on the instrumentation setup can be found in Dana et al. (2017). 

The turbine nacelle's wind vane signal was modified using a frequency modulation device with a dedicated user interface for programming yaw-offset schedules of discrete offset values and durations. In no other way was the turbine or its controller manipulated. The turbine was set to cycle at 1 h intervals between the baseline setting, i.e., a 0 • yaw offset, and a nonzero offset.

Title: A SCADA-Informed Framework Combining Machine Learning and Wind Speed Correction for Yaw Misalignment Detection
Snippet: This study presented a SCADA-only framework for detecting static yaw misalignment in operating wind turbines. The approach embeds a parametric yaw loss function into a Gaussian Process power curve model, enabling direct estimation of static yaw offsets from trained model parameters while explicitly accounting for observation uncertainty. A consensus-based wind speed correction step is incorporated to mitigate yaw-dependent biases in nacelle anemometer measurements. Application to the Kelmarsh wind farm yields offset estimates consistent in sign and magnitude across turbines and AEP losses in line with literature values, demonstrating the potential of the framework for scalable, data-driven yaw misalignment detection. Ongoing and future work, as discussed above, focuses on external validation, relaxing the symmetry assumption of the loss function, and developing uncertainty-aware estimates of the inferred yaw offsets.

Title: Deviation of drive torque and rotational speed of a wind turbine drivetrain between test bench and wind turbine simulations
Snippet: The correct representation of the loads acting at the hub and throughout the drivetrain tested at system test benches is important as these are used to validate the wind turbine simulation models and to predict the drivetrain's behaviour of the erected wind turbine. The differences between erected wind turbine (wind turbine with rotor and tower) and test bench (nacelle with drive unit and wind load unit) lead to deviations in hub loads. This paper focusses on the deviations of the hub torque and rotational speed between erected wind turbine and bench tests using simulation models. Hub torque and rotational speed values are generally represented well by the test bench drive unit. The torque time series values of the field application are maximum 5 % higher than at the test bench for low wind speeds and maximum 2 % higher compared to the rated torque. The deviations can result from the way the torque is applied at the test bench as the drive unit sets the rotational speed and the DUT sets the corresponding torque: The drivetrain efficiency of the aerodynamic simulation is lower than the test bench drivetrain efficiency as the drivetrain efficiency in the aerodynamic simulation also includes losses from e.g. the pitch drives, the converter etc. Thus, the aerodynamic torque must be higher to reach the same generator torque. Another reason is the different inertias of the drivetrains of the erected wind turbine and the test bench. This lower torque at the test bench leads to an underestimation of the acting component loads and displacements in the drivetrain at the test bench relative to the erected wind turbine and thus needs to be investigated in the future for the gearbox components. 

Future work will also compare the accuracy of the representation of thrust, lateral forces and bending moments as these are the relevant loads for the main bearings. Further work will focus also on the deviations in the drivetrain response to the acting loads evaluating accelerations, displacements and loads in the drivetrain using MBS and FEM. Finally, the goal is to identify the reasons for the deviations IOP Publishing doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2767/4/042013 10 which may lie in the load application system or the stiffness of the connections to the test bench. The following step will be the investigation of design adjustments of the test bench to reduce these deviations.

Title: Wind turbine drivetrains: state-of-the-art technologies and future development trends
Snippet: Abstract. This paper presents the state-of-the-art technologies and development trends of wind turbine drivetrains – the energy conversion systems transferring the kinetic energy of the wind to electrical energy – in different stages of their life cycle: design, manufacturing, installation, operation, lifetime extension, decommissioning, and recycling. Offshore development and digitalization are also a focal point in this study. The main aim of this article is to review the drivetrain technology development as well as to identify future challenges and research gaps. Drivetrain in this context includes the whole power conversion system: main bearing, shafts, gearbox, generator, and power converter. The paper discusses current design technologies for each component along with advantages and disadvantages. The discussion of the operation phase highlights the condition monitoring methods currently employed by the industry as well as emerging areas. This article also illustrates the multidisciplinary aspect of wind turbine drivetrains, which emphasizes the need for more interdisciplinary research and collaboration.

Title: Monitoring Wind Turbine Loading Using Power Converter Signals
Snippet: The ability to detect faults and predict loads on a wind turbine drivetrain's mechanical components cost-effectively is critical to making the cost of wind energy competitive. In order to investigate whether this is possible using the readily available power converter current signals, an existing permanent magnet synchronous generator based wind energy conversion system computer model was modified to include a grid-side converter (GSC) for an improved converter model and a gearbox. The GSC maintains a constant DC link voltage via vector control. The gearbox was modelled as a 3-mass model to allow faults to be included. Gusts and gearbox faults were introduced to investigate the ability of the machine side converter (MSC) current (Iq) to detect and quantify loads on the mechanical components. In this model, gearbox faults were not detectable in the Iq signal due to shaft stiffness and damping interaction. However, a model that predicts the load change on mechanical wind turbine components using Iq was developed and verified using synthetic and real wind data.

Title: Field validation of dynamic mechanical torque measurements using fiber-optic strain sensors for geared wind turbines
Snippet: Wind turbine power ratings, rotor diameters, and hub heights have grown significantly to reduce the cost of wind energy [1]. The wind turbine drivetrain converts mechanical power to electrical power and transmits the rotor loads to the bedplate and tower [2]; it makes an appreciable contribution to the capital expenditure of the turbine [3]. Many wind turbine drivetrains use gearboxes to lower the capital cost of the drivetrain, but its reliability is essential and remains a top priority because gearbox failures cause long downtime with costly repairs and contribute appreciably to the turbine operation and maintenance costs [4][5][6]. Thanks to internationally recognized gearbox wind turbine design standards like IEC 61400-4 and AGMA 6006 and collaborative efforts like the Drivetrain Reliability Collaborative between turbine manufacturers, gearbox designers, bearing suppliers, and research institutions like the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and Argonne National Laboratory, average annual gearbox failure rates for the U.S. land-based fleet have dropped from 5% to 10% 20 years ago [7] to 2.5% more recently [8]. Yet, there is room for improvement because gearboxes still generally do not reach their desired design life [9]. These standards have placed greater rigor on the design and gearbox verification process, including the effects of rotor nontorque loads [10], transient events [11,12], and electrical currents [13]. However, the rapid pace at which torque density requirements have risen has led to increasingly complex and lightweight designs with new reliability challenges and additional requirements, such as complying with stricter noise demands and more prominent dynamic interactions. 

Accurate knowledge of the dynamic mechanical torque in wind turbine gearboxes is essential to complying with these requirements and improving their reliability. Dynamic mechanical torque measurements of every gearbox in a fleet can enhance drivetrain usage monitoring because the consumed fatigue life can be assessed more precisely using the measured torque values throughout their entire commercial operation. Dynamic torque measurements can also potentially be used by the wind turbine controller for improved wind turbine control to achieve a reduction of torque oscillations (i.e., torsional damping). Additionally, dynamic mechanical torque measurements can be used to quantify drivetrain efficiency.

Title: Influence of drivetrain efficiency determination on the torque control of wind turbines
Snippet: Decreasing the levelized cost of energy is a major design objective for wind turbines. Accordingly, the control is generally optimized to achieve a high energy production and a high-power coefficient. In partial load range, speed and torque are controlled via the generator torque but the rotor torque determines the power coefficient of the turbine. High uncertainties for the uncalibrated low-speed shaft torque measurement and varying drivetrain efficiencies which depend on the speed, load and temperature lead to a torque control error that reduces the power coefficient of the wind turbine. In this paper the rotor torque control error and the impact on the power coefficient of wind turbines is quantified. For this purpose, the variation of drivetrain efficiency is analyzed. An efficiency model for the wind turbine drivetrain is build and validated on the test bench. Then, the influence of the drivetrain speed, torque loads, non-torque loads, and temperature on the efficiency is quantified. Finally, the influence of the rotor torque control error on the power coefficient was simulated with an aerodynamic model. The results show that of all examined influences only torque and temperature significantly impacting the efficiency leading to rotor torque control errors that reduce the power coefficient and consequently increase the levelized cost of energy. Improved efficiency measurement on WT test benches or drivetrain efficiency modelling can reduce the rotor torque control error and therefore decrease the LCOE. The correct representation of the loads acting at the hub and throughout the drivetrain tested at system test benches is important as these are used to validate the wind turbine simulation models and to predict the drivetrain's behaviour of the erected wind turbine. snippet.text: The ability to detect faults and predict loads on a wind turbine drivetrain's mechanical components cost-effectively is critical to making the cost of wind energy competitive. In order to investigate whether this is possible using the readily available power converter current signals, an existing permanent magnet synchronous generator based wind energy conversion system computer model was modified to include a grid-side converter (GSC) for an improved converter model and a gearbox. snippet.text:
Wind turbine power ratings, rotor diameters, and hub heights have grown significantly to reduce the cost of wind energy [1]. The wind turbine drivetrain converts mechanical power to electrical power and transmits the rotor loads to the bedplate and tower [2]; it makes an appreciable contribution to the capital expenditure of the turbine [3]. Many wind turbine drivetrains use gearboxes to lower the capital cost of the drivetrain, but its reliability is essential and remains a top priority because gearbox failures cause long downtime with costly repairs and contribute appreciably to the turbine operation and maintenance costs [4][5][6]. Thanks to internationally recognized gearbox wind turbine design standards like IEC 61400-4 and AGMA 6006 and collaborative efforts like the Drivetrain Reliability Collaborative between turbine manufacturers, gearbox designers, bearing suppliers, and research institutions like the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) and Argonne National Laboratory, average annual gearbox failure rates for the U.S. land-based fleet have dropped from 5% to 10% 20 years ago [7] to 2.5% more recently [8]. Yet, there is room for improvement because gearboxes still generally do not reach their desired design life [9]. These standards have placed greater rigor on the design and gearbox verification process, including the effects of rotor nontorque loads [10], transient events [11,12], and electrical currents [13]. However, the rapid pace at which torque density requirements have risen has led to increasingly complex and lightweight designs with new reliability challenges and additional requirements, such as complying with stricter noise demands and more prominent dynamic interactions. 

Accurate knowledge of the dynamic mechanical torque in wind turbine gearboxes is essential to complying with these requirements and improving their reliability. Dynamic mechanical torque measurements of every gearbox in a fleet can enhance drivetrain usage monitoring because the consumed fatigue life can be assessed more precisely using the measured torque values throughout their entire commercial operation. Dynamic torque measurements can also potentially be used by the wind turbine controller for improved wind turbine control to achieve a reduction of torque oscillations (i.e., torsional damping). Additionally, dynamic mechanical torque measurements can be used to quantify drivetrain efficiency.

snippet.text: Decreasing the levelized cost of energy is a major design objective for wind turbines. Accordingly, the control is generally optimized to achieve a high energy production and a high-power coefficient. In partial load range, speed and torque are controlled via the generator torque but the rotor torque determines the power coefficient of the turbine. High uncertainties for the uncalibrated low-speed shaft torque measurement and varying drivetrain efficiencies which depend on the speed, load and temperature lead to a torque control error that reduces the power coefficient of the wind turbine. In this paper the rotor torque control error and the impact on the power coefficient of wind turbines is quantified. For this purpose, the variation of drivetrain efficiency is analyzed. An efficiency model for the wind turbine drivetrain is build and validated on the test bench. Then, the influence of the drivetrain speed, torque loads, non-torque loads, and temperature on the efficiency is quantified. Finally, the influence of the rotor torque control error on the power coefficient was simulated with an aerodynamic model. The results show that of all examined influences only torque and temperature significantly impacting the efficiency leading to rotor torque control errors that reduce the power coefficient and consequently increase the levelized cost of energy. Improved efficiency measurement on WT test benches or drivetrain efficiency modelling can reduce the rotor torque control error and therefore decrease the LCOE. attempts.answer:
Summary answer
- Causally, efficiency (power coefficient Cp) is maximized at a particular tip‑speed ratio (TSR) set by the blade’s aerodynamics; moving the rotor faster or slower than this optimal TSR, without redesign or control, reduces Cp through angle‑of‑attack and stall effects that degrade lift and increase drag. <cite id="72e87897-1">From controlled experiments on a horizontal‑axis model turbine, Cp rises with TSR to a peak around λ≈7.4 and then declines, and changing pitch away from optimal lowers Cp by moving blade elements into suboptimal or stalled regimes</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Wind‑tunnel tests similarly show Cp increases with TSR to a maximum and then decreases; in the low‑TSR region angle of attack is high, lift falls and drag rises, lowering Cp, while in the high‑TSR region angle of attack is too low for effective energy capture</cite>. 
- However, observed correlations between higher TSR and higher Cp in the field are often confounded by blade design and control: chord, solidity, number of blades, airfoil, and twist determine the optimal λ and the shape of Cp(λ); modern controllers regulate pitch and rotational speed to keep TSR near its design optimum as wind varies. Increasing TSR without redesign—i.e., overspeeding a given blade—typically moves operation off the optimal Cp(λ) peak and reduces efficiency or risks stall/dynamic loads. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">With increasing chord length, the maximum Cp can increase but the optimal TSR shifts to lower values; beyond a chord Reynolds number threshold, further chord increases yield marginal Cp gains</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing the number of blades reduces maximum Cp and shifts Cp(λ) left, i.e., changes the optimal TSR and working range</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">The optimal Cp occurs at a specific λ and pitch; deviations in either reduce Cp due to angle‑of‑attack misalignment relative to the blade element’s lift/drag optimum</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">For all wind turbines, Cp is a nonlinear function of TSR that increases, peaks, and then decreases; after design, the maximum Cp and its λ are used to tune controllers to maintain the optimal TSR</cite>.

Definitions and mechanism
- TSR (λ) is the ratio of blade tip speed to free‑stream wind speed; Cp is a nonlinear function of λ and pitch, with a single maximum in Region 2 for modern HAWTs. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Cp is a nonlinear function of TSR, rising then falling, and designers identify Cpmax and λopt to guide controllers that regulate TSR</cite> <cite id="72e87897-0">The power coefficient is a function of TSR and pitch angle; standard models and curves are used to relate Cp to λ and β</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, increasing TSR changes the relative inflow angle across the span: at low λ the angle of attack is high (risking stall), near optimal λ aligns angle of attack with favorable lift/drag, and at high λ it becomes too low, reducing the lift‑to‑drag contribution per element and lowering Cp. <cite id="72e87897-1">At low λ the inflow angle is large and angle of attack approaches the optimum for Cp; at high λ the inflow angle is small, angle of attack is insufficient for lift or reduces the rotational component of lift, lowering Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">As λ increases, angle of attack increases at low λ (excess angle of attack reduces lift and increases drag), Cp peaks and then decreases; at higher λ angle of attack is too low for effective energy capture</cite>.

Causal evidence isolating TSR: controlled experiments and swept‑parameter studies
- Experiments that sweep TSR at fixed geometry show the canonical Cp(λ) curve with a single peak and demonstrate that moving away from optimal λ reduces Cp, consistent with angle‑of‑attack physics. <cite id="72e87897-1">For a model HAWT at U=10 m/s, Cp rises with λ to a maximum at λ=7.4 (θ=0° pitch) and falls as λ or pitch deviates from this point; increasing or decreasing pitch from optimal lowers the maximum Cp by misaligning angle of attack</cite> <cite id="72e87897-2">Under oblique inflow, Cp peaks at λ=7.4 with θ=0° and Cp decreases as yaw changes; thrust behavior varies with λ and yaw, reflecting periodic angle‑of‑attack changes that modulate loading</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Across wind speeds of 7–10 m/s, Cp increases with λ to a peak and then decreases; at each speed the peak Cp and optimal λ are reported (e.g., Cp=0.408 at λ=7.43 at 10 m/s), and the mechanism is linked to angle‑of‑attack transitions</cite>.
- Parameter sweeps over blade geometry confirm that the relationship between Cp and TSR is set by design: changing chord, solidity, and number of blades moves the Cp(λ) curve left/right and changes Cpmax, implying that a “higher λ yields higher Cp” observation without controlling geometry is confounded by design choices that re‑locate the optimum. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing chord length raises maximum Cp but decreases optimal TSR; as chord Reynolds number grows beyond a threshold, gains in Cp saturate or decline, and the optimal λ shifts left</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing the number of blades gradually reduces Cp and shifts the optimal TSR lower while narrowing the effective operating range</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Changing chord length produced little difference in maximum Cp for an open VAWT but shifted the λ range where Cpmax occurred; lower solidity shifted Cpmax to higher λ, consistent with solidity’s role in setting the optimal TSR</cite>.

Blade design confounders: chord, twist, airfoil, and structural limits
- Optimal λ and Cpmax are co‑determined by chord/twist distributions, airfoil lift/drag curves, and Reynolds numbers. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers identify λopt and Cpmax for a given rotor and then use controllers to maintain λopt; this follows from Cp being a function of λ and aerodynamic loading of the blade elements</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">BEM‑based blade design shows how elementwise radius, partial λ, chord, and flow angle determine how lift and power scale; optimization of twist and chord distributions sets the element angles of attack and thus the achievable Cpmax at a design λ</cite>. 
- Empirical studies show that airfoil family and geometric parameters shift the Cp(λ) curve and the peak. <cite id="72e87897-3">For different asymmetric airfoils, torque and power increase with λ to a peak; under a given airfoil, increasing camber raises power up to an extent, after which further camber yields muted changes, reflecting how airfoil properties and TSR interact to set Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-3">The mapping from angle of attack (which depends on λ and phase) to Cp shows that a defined range of −30° to 30° governs backflow and loading, linking geometric parameters to λ‑dependent efficiency</cite>.
- Structural and dynamic limits often force operation at TSRs below the theoretical optimum, and increasing TSR beyond design constraints can degrade Cp or damage the machine. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">As chord increases, interactions in blade vortex shedding enhance when Reynolds number effects saturate, limiting Cp gains; increasing solidity/number of blades narrows and shifts Cp(λ) left, and raises thrust, underscoring trade‑offs in raising λ</cite>.

Operational confounders: control, region‑of‑operation, and pitch
- Controllers explicitly tie efficiency to λ by tracking the design Cp(λ) peak; pitch regulation adjusts angle of attack so that λ remains optimal as wind speed and aerodynamic conditions change. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">After rotor design, the maximum Cp and its λ are identified and used to tune control to maintain optimum λ regardless of wind speed</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Measured Cp(λ) peaks at λ≈7.4 with zero pitch; moving pitch away from zero lowers Cp by degrading angle of attack, confirming the control objective of maintaining λopt and βopt</cite>.
- In practice, “higher TSR” is achieved either by redesigning for a higher λopt (longer blades, optimized twist/chord distributions) or by control at a fixed geometry; the correlation between higher TSR and higher Cp is therefore confounded by whether the increase in λ is a design shift or a controlled hold‑at‑optimum versus an overspeed away from the Cp peak. <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">Optimization of twist/chord sets elementwise flow angle and partial λ to maximize Cp at a target operating point, directly coupling design choices to the achievable λopt and Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Experimental Cp(λ) peaks around λ≈7.2–7.5 at 7–10 m/s with corresponding Cp≈0.39–0.41; attempts to force higher λ without changing aerodynamics reduce Cp due to angle‑of‑attack misalignment</cite>.

Do modern turbines operate at very high λ with improved Cp? Trade‑offs at high λ (2020–2025)
- Contemporary HAWTs commonly target λ≈6–8 in Region 2, with Cpmax≈0.4–0.5 depending on design; claims of “higher Cp at higher λ” without redesign are inconsistent with experiments that show Cp declines beyond λopt due to angle‑of‑attack loss. <cite id="72e87897-4">Across wind speeds 7–10 m/s, peak Cp≈0.408 occurs at λ≈7.43; beyond this, increasing λ reduces Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Maximum Cp occurs at λ≈7.4 with θ=0°; deviations in λ or pitch reduce Cp by moving angle of attack out of the favorable range</cite>. 
- Some studies suggest that for fixed geometries with lower solidity or shorter chords, the λ at which Cpmax occurs shifts higher, but maximum Cp may not increase and often increases only modestly. <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Changing chord length had little effect on maximum Cp for an open VAWT, while shifting the Cpmax to higher λ; similar trends with wind lenses showed power augmentation but the same qualitative dependence</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">As chord increases, maximal utilization coefficient increases but the optimal λ decreases; beyond a Reynolds threshold, Cp gains saturate, so “higher λ improves Cp” is not a general rule</cite>. 
- High TSR regimes also raise dynamic stall and structural loading risks, which constrain operation and can reduce effective efficiency if λ must be limited to avoid damage. <cite id="72e87897-2">Under oblique inflow and yaw offsets, angle of attack varies periodically with rotation; larger yaw amplifies angle‑of‑attack changes and modulates thrust and power gradients with λ, underscoring dynamic sensitivity and load–efficiency trade‑offs</cite>.

Putting it together: causal interpretation vs. confounding
- Causal interpretation: For a given blade geometry and airfoil family, there is an optimal λ that maximizes Cp; operating at that λ with appropriate pitch yields the highest aerodynamic efficiency. Moving the rotor faster or slower without redesign reduces Cp via angle‑of‑attack misalignment and associated lift/drag changes. <cite id="72e87897-4">Cp increases with TSR to a peak then decreases; at low λ high angle of attack reduces lift and increases drag, and at high λ angle of attack is too low, lowering Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Maximum Cp occurs at a specific TSR and pitch; deviations reduce Cp by misaligning angle of attack</cite>.
- Confounding by blade design: Empirical correlations that “higher TSR improves Cp” in the field can reflect design choices (chord, twist, number of blades, airfoil) that shift λopt and Cpmax. A blade designed for higher λ (e.g., optimized chord/twist for higher, thinner elements) can exhibit higher Cp at elevated λ; for other geometries, pushing λ higher may not raise Cp and can even reduce it or narrow the operating range. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing chord can increase Cpmax but lowers λopt; increasing solidity/number of blades reduces Cpmax and shifts λopt left</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Lower solidity shifts Cpmax to higher λ with little change in maximum Cp; thus, higher λ alone does not guarantee higher Cp</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers explicitly determine λopt and Cpmax and then tune controllers to hold λopt, so observed “higher λ → higher Cp” trends without controlling design are confounded by design‑set λopt</cite>.
- Role of control: Modern turbines use MPPT and pitch to hold TSR near its design optimum across wind speeds; thus, increases in measured TSR often coincide with operating point tracking of the Cp peak rather than a causal improvement in aerodynamic efficiency from spinning faster. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Controllers maintain optimum λ regardless of wind speed to achieve Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Measured Cp(λ) confirms the optimum around λ≈7.4 with zero pitch; moving pitch or λ away lowers Cp</cite>.

Practical implications (2020–2025)
- If your goal is to improve conversion efficiency:
  - Redesign with chord/twist distributions and airfoil selection that raise Cpmax at the intended operating λ and wind regime; quantify how much Cpmax rises and at what λopt. <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">Elementwise optimization of twist and chord sets flow angle and partial λ to maximize Cp at a design point</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Changes in chord and solidity can increase Cpmax or shift λopt; plan accordingly</cite>.
  - Use control to hold TSR near λopt as wind varies; avoid overspeeding into high‑λ regimes without aerodynamic redesign, as Cp will fall due to angle‑of‑attack loss. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Control maintains λopt to achieve Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Beyond λ≈7.4, Cp declines because angle of attack is no longer optimal</cite>.
  - Be mindful of structural and dynamic limits; if λ must be capped for loads or stability, efficiency gains from “higher λ” are capped or reversed, and trade‑offs with thrust/loading may worsen energy capture. <cite id="72e87897-2">Angle‑of‑attack variations and yaw sensitivity imply that pushing λ without addressing loads/instability reduces effective Cp</cite>.

Bottom line
- Increasing TSR causally improves aerodynamic conversion efficiency only when it moves the operating point closer to the blade’s optimal angle of attack; otherwise—i.e., without redesign—higher TSR typically moves operation away from the Cp peak and reduces efficiency. Observed “higher TSR, higher Cp” correlations in practice are commonly confounded by blade design parameters (chord, twist, solidity/number of blades, airfoil) and by control strategies that regulate TSR to track the design optimum. <cite id="72e87897-4">Cp rises with TSR to a peak and then falls due to angle‑of‑attack and drag effects</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Chord and solidity redesigns can raise Cpmax and shift λopt; beyond thresholds, gains saturate or decline</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers and controllers explicitly target the TSR and pitch that maximize Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Deviations in TSR or pitch from the optimum reduce Cp</cite>.

I will also look for field/experimental evidence that operating above/below optimal TSR reduces Cp, and for discussions of confounders (Reynolds number, chord/twist selection).

Sufficiency check and plan:
I have gathered recent (2020–2025) evidence that: (i) Cp is a nonlinear function of TSR with a single peak; (ii) experiments vary TSR at fixed geometry and show Cp rises to an optimal TSR then falls, with mechanistic explanations via angle of attack, lift/drag, and stall; (iii) blade design parameters (chord, number of blades/solidity, airfoil) shift the Cp(λ) curve and set the optimal TSR; and (iv) controllers regulate pitch and speed to hold TSR near its design optimum to maximize Cp. I also found that increasing TSR without redesign (e.g., overspeeding) moves operation out of the optimal angle-of-attack range, reducing Cp, and that structural/dynamic effects can limit TSR well above the ideal value. Conflicts are minor and reflect geometry/airfoil differences (optimal λ often 6–8 for HAWT in Region 2, sometimes higher in certain designs). I will structure the answer with: (1) definitions and causal graph; (2) experimental evidence isolating TSR effects; (3) design confounders (chord, twist, solidity) and how they set optimal λ; (4) operational confounders (pitch, region-of-operation); (5) high TSR trade-offs and whether efficiency still improves; (6) synthesis and practical guidance. I will cite each evidence-backed claim.
