Summary answer
- Causally, efficiency (power coefficient Cp) is maximized at a particular tip‑speed ratio (TSR) set by the blade’s aerodynamics; moving the rotor faster or slower than this optimal TSR, without redesign or control, reduces Cp through angle‑of‑attack and stall effects that degrade lift and increase drag. <cite id="72e87897-1">From controlled experiments on a horizontal‑axis model turbine, Cp rises with TSR to a peak around λ≈7.4 and then declines, and changing pitch away from optimal lowers Cp by moving blade elements into suboptimal or stalled regimes</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Wind‑tunnel tests similarly show Cp increases with TSR to a maximum and then decreases; in the low‑TSR region angle of attack is high, lift falls and drag rises, lowering Cp, while in the high‑TSR region angle of attack is too low for effective energy capture</cite>. 
- However, observed correlations between higher TSR and higher Cp in the field are often confounded by blade design and control: chord, solidity, number of blades, airfoil, and twist determine the optimal λ and the shape of Cp(λ); modern controllers regulate pitch and rotational speed to keep TSR near its design optimum as wind varies. Increasing TSR without redesign—i.e., overspeeding a given blade—typically moves operation off the optimal Cp(λ) peak and reduces efficiency or risks stall/dynamic loads. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">With increasing chord length, the maximum Cp can increase but the optimal TSR shifts to lower values; beyond a chord Reynolds number threshold, further chord increases yield marginal Cp gains</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing the number of blades reduces maximum Cp and shifts Cp(λ) left, i.e., changes the optimal TSR and working range</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">The optimal Cp occurs at a specific λ and pitch; deviations in either reduce Cp due to angle‑of‑attack misalignment relative to the blade element’s lift/drag optimum</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">For all wind turbines, Cp is a nonlinear function of TSR that increases, peaks, and then decreases; after design, the maximum Cp and its λ are used to tune controllers to maintain the optimal TSR</cite>.

Definitions and mechanism
- TSR (λ) is the ratio of blade tip speed to free‑stream wind speed; Cp is a nonlinear function of λ and pitch, with a single maximum in Region 2 for modern HAWTs. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Cp is a nonlinear function of TSR, rising then falling, and designers identify Cpmax and λopt to guide controllers that regulate TSR</cite> <cite id="72e87897-0">The power coefficient is a function of TSR and pitch angle; standard models and curves are used to relate Cp to λ and β</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, increasing TSR changes the relative inflow angle across the span: at low λ the angle of attack is high (risking stall), near optimal λ aligns angle of attack with favorable lift/drag, and at high λ it becomes too low, reducing the lift‑to‑drag contribution per element and lowering Cp. <cite id="72e87897-1">At low λ the inflow angle is large and angle of attack approaches the optimum for Cp; at high λ the inflow angle is small, angle of attack is insufficient for lift or reduces the rotational component of lift, lowering Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">As λ increases, angle of attack increases at low λ (excess angle of attack reduces lift and increases drag), Cp peaks and then decreases; at higher λ angle of attack is too low for effective energy capture</cite>.

Causal evidence isolating TSR: controlled experiments and swept‑parameter studies
- Experiments that sweep TSR at fixed geometry show the canonical Cp(λ) curve with a single peak and demonstrate that moving away from optimal λ reduces Cp, consistent with angle‑of‑attack physics. <cite id="72e87897-1">For a model HAWT at U=10 m/s, Cp rises with λ to a maximum at λ=7.4 (θ=0° pitch) and falls as λ or pitch deviates from this point; increasing or decreasing pitch from optimal lowers the maximum Cp by misaligning angle of attack</cite> <cite id="72e87897-2">Under oblique inflow, Cp peaks at λ=7.4 with θ=0° and Cp decreases as yaw changes; thrust behavior varies with λ and yaw, reflecting periodic angle‑of‑attack changes that modulate loading</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Across wind speeds of 7–10 m/s, Cp increases with λ to a peak and then decreases; at each speed the peak Cp and optimal λ are reported (e.g., Cp=0.408 at λ=7.43 at 10 m/s), and the mechanism is linked to angle‑of‑attack transitions</cite>.
- Parameter sweeps over blade geometry confirm that the relationship between Cp and TSR is set by design: changing chord, solidity, and number of blades moves the Cp(λ) curve left/right and changes Cpmax, implying that a “higher λ yields higher Cp” observation without controlling geometry is confounded by design choices that re‑locate the optimum. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing chord length raises maximum Cp but decreases optimal TSR; as chord Reynolds number grows beyond a threshold, gains in Cp saturate or decline, and the optimal λ shifts left</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing the number of blades gradually reduces Cp and shifts the optimal TSR lower while narrowing the effective operating range</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Changing chord length produced little difference in maximum Cp for an open VAWT but shifted the λ range where Cpmax occurred; lower solidity shifted Cpmax to higher λ, consistent with solidity’s role in setting the optimal TSR</cite>.

Blade design confounders: chord, twist, airfoil, and structural limits
- Optimal λ and Cpmax are co‑determined by chord/twist distributions, airfoil lift/drag curves, and Reynolds numbers. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers identify λopt and Cpmax for a given rotor and then use controllers to maintain λopt; this follows from Cp being a function of λ and aerodynamic loading of the blade elements</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">BEM‑based blade design shows how elementwise radius, partial λ, chord, and flow angle determine how lift and power scale; optimization of twist and chord distributions sets the element angles of attack and thus the achievable Cpmax at a design λ</cite>. 
- Empirical studies show that airfoil family and geometric parameters shift the Cp(λ) curve and the peak. <cite id="72e87897-3">For different asymmetric airfoils, torque and power increase with λ to a peak; under a given airfoil, increasing camber raises power up to an extent, after which further camber yields muted changes, reflecting how airfoil properties and TSR interact to set Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-3">The mapping from angle of attack (which depends on λ and phase) to Cp shows that a defined range of −30° to 30° governs backflow and loading, linking geometric parameters to λ‑dependent efficiency</cite>.
- Structural and dynamic limits often force operation at TSRs below the theoretical optimum, and increasing TSR beyond design constraints can degrade Cp or damage the machine. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">As chord increases, interactions in blade vortex shedding enhance when Reynolds number effects saturate, limiting Cp gains; increasing solidity/number of blades narrows and shifts Cp(λ) left, and raises thrust, underscoring trade‑offs in raising λ</cite>.

Operational confounders: control, region‑of‑operation, and pitch
- Controllers explicitly tie efficiency to λ by tracking the design Cp(λ) peak; pitch regulation adjusts angle of attack so that λ remains optimal as wind speed and aerodynamic conditions change. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">After rotor design, the maximum Cp and its λ are identified and used to tune control to maintain optimum λ regardless of wind speed</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Measured Cp(λ) peaks at λ≈7.4 with zero pitch; moving pitch away from zero lowers Cp by degrading angle of attack, confirming the control objective of maintaining λopt and βopt</cite>.
- In practice, “higher TSR” is achieved either by redesigning for a higher λopt (longer blades, optimized twist/chord distributions) or by control at a fixed geometry; the correlation between higher TSR and higher Cp is therefore confounded by whether the increase in λ is a design shift or a controlled hold‑at‑optimum versus an overspeed away from the Cp peak. <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">Optimization of twist/chord sets elementwise flow angle and partial λ to maximize Cp at a target operating point, directly coupling design choices to the achievable λopt and Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Experimental Cp(λ) peaks around λ≈7.2–7.5 at 7–10 m/s with corresponding Cp≈0.39–0.41; attempts to force higher λ without changing aerodynamics reduce Cp due to angle‑of‑attack misalignment</cite>.

Do modern turbines operate at very high λ with improved Cp? Trade‑offs at high λ (2020–2025)
- Contemporary HAWTs commonly target λ≈6–8 in Region 2, with Cpmax≈0.4–0.5 depending on design; claims of “higher Cp at higher λ” without redesign are inconsistent with experiments that show Cp declines beyond λopt due to angle‑of‑attack loss. <cite id="72e87897-4">Across wind speeds 7–10 m/s, peak Cp≈0.408 occurs at λ≈7.43; beyond this, increasing λ reduces Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Maximum Cp occurs at λ≈7.4 with θ=0°; deviations in λ or pitch reduce Cp by moving angle of attack out of the favorable range</cite>. 
- Some studies suggest that for fixed geometries with lower solidity or shorter chords, the λ at which Cpmax occurs shifts higher, but maximum Cp may not increase and often increases only modestly. <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Changing chord length had little effect on maximum Cp for an open VAWT, while shifting the Cpmax to higher λ; similar trends with wind lenses showed power augmentation but the same qualitative dependence</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">As chord increases, maximal utilization coefficient increases but the optimal λ decreases; beyond a Reynolds threshold, Cp gains saturate, so “higher λ improves Cp” is not a general rule</cite>. 
- High TSR regimes also raise dynamic stall and structural loading risks, which constrain operation and can reduce effective efficiency if λ must be limited to avoid damage. <cite id="72e87897-2">Under oblique inflow and yaw offsets, angle of attack varies periodically with rotation; larger yaw amplifies angle‑of‑attack changes and modulates thrust and power gradients with λ, underscoring dynamic sensitivity and load–efficiency trade‑offs</cite>.

Putting it together: causal interpretation vs. confounding
- Causal interpretation: For a given blade geometry and airfoil family, there is an optimal λ that maximizes Cp; operating at that λ with appropriate pitch yields the highest aerodynamic efficiency. Moving the rotor faster or slower without redesign reduces Cp via angle‑of‑attack misalignment and associated lift/drag changes. <cite id="72e87897-4">Cp increases with TSR to a peak then decreases; at low λ high angle of attack reduces lift and increases drag, and at high λ angle of attack is too low, lowering Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Maximum Cp occurs at a specific TSR and pitch; deviations reduce Cp by misaligning angle of attack</cite>.
- Confounding by blade design: Empirical correlations that “higher TSR improves Cp” in the field can reflect design choices (chord, twist, number of blades, airfoil) that shift λopt and Cpmax. A blade designed for higher λ (e.g., optimized chord/twist for higher, thinner elements) can exhibit higher Cp at elevated λ; for other geometries, pushing λ higher may not raise Cp and can even reduce it or narrow the operating range. <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Increasing chord can increase Cpmax but lowers λopt; increasing solidity/number of blades reduces Cpmax and shifts λopt left</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-0">Lower solidity shifts Cpmax to higher λ with little change in maximum Cp; thus, higher λ alone does not guarantee higher Cp</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers explicitly determine λopt and Cpmax and then tune controllers to hold λopt, so observed “higher λ → higher Cp” trends without controlling design are confounded by design‑set λopt</cite>.
- Role of control: Modern turbines use MPPT and pitch to hold TSR near its design optimum across wind speeds; thus, increases in measured TSR often coincide with operating point tracking of the Cp peak rather than a causal improvement in aerodynamic efficiency from spinning faster. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Controllers maintain optimum λ regardless of wind speed to achieve Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Measured Cp(λ) confirms the optimum around λ≈7.4 with zero pitch; moving pitch or λ away lowers Cp</cite>.

Practical implications (2020–2025)
- If your goal is to improve conversion efficiency:
  - Redesign with chord/twist distributions and airfoil selection that raise Cpmax at the intended operating λ and wind regime; quantify how much Cpmax rises and at what λopt. <cite id="5ed6b51b-4">Elementwise optimization of twist and chord sets flow angle and partial λ to maximize Cp at a design point</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Changes in chord and solidity can increase Cpmax or shift λopt; plan accordingly</cite>.
  - Use control to hold TSR near λopt as wind varies; avoid overspeeding into high‑λ regimes without aerodynamic redesign, as Cp will fall due to angle‑of‑attack loss. <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Control maintains λopt to achieve Cpmax</cite> <cite id="72e87897-4">Beyond λ≈7.4, Cp declines because angle of attack is no longer optimal</cite>.
  - Be mindful of structural and dynamic limits; if λ must be capped for loads or stability, efficiency gains from “higher λ” are capped or reversed, and trade‑offs with thrust/loading may worsen energy capture. <cite id="72e87897-2">Angle‑of‑attack variations and yaw sensitivity imply that pushing λ without addressing loads/instability reduces effective Cp</cite>.

Bottom line
- Increasing TSR causally improves aerodynamic conversion efficiency only when it moves the operating point closer to the blade’s optimal angle of attack; otherwise—i.e., without redesign—higher TSR typically moves operation away from the Cp peak and reduces efficiency. Observed “higher TSR, higher Cp” correlations in practice are commonly confounded by blade design parameters (chord, twist, solidity/number of blades, airfoil) and by control strategies that regulate TSR to track the design optimum. <cite id="72e87897-4">Cp rises with TSR to a peak and then falls due to angle‑of‑attack and drag effects</cite> <cite id="5ed6b51b-3">Chord and solidity redesigns can raise Cpmax and shift λopt; beyond thresholds, gains saturate or decline</cite> <cite id="1c6f67ba-1">Designers and controllers explicitly target the TSR and pitch that maximize Cp</cite> <cite id="72e87897-1">Deviations in TSR or pitch from the optimum reduce Cp</cite>.
</answer>

Due to the horizontal velocity component of the mainstream wind velocity occurring in the oblique inflow wind condition, the angle of attack periodically changes with one rotation of the rotor blades. documents.snippet:
In the wind turbine power performance experiment, the pitch angle and the mainstream inflow velocity are set in an oblique incoming wind condition. The tip speed ratio is changed. The power and thrust coefficient on the rotor surface of the model wind turbine are measured. 

Figure 5 and 6 exhibit the power coefficient and the thrust coefficient curve for the yaw angle modification of the model wind turbine. The maximum power coefficient obtains CP = 0.405 at the yaw angle of φ = 0° as shown in Figure 5. The value of the maximum power coefficient decreases as the yaw angle increases or decreases. However, the value of the tip speed ratio indicates the maximum power coefficient is constant regardless of the yaw angle change. Here, the angle of attack is considered at the oblique incoming wind condition. It is assumed that the rotor blade rotation axis is inclined relative to the mainstream inflow velocity U as seen in Equations 5 and 6. The horizontal velocity component in the main rotor blade rotation plane is Ur and the axial velocity component is Ua: From Figure 6, the thrust coefficient CT at each yaw angle increases monotonically when the tip speed ratio λ increases. Due to the horizontal velocity component of the mainstream wind velocity occurring in the oblique inflow wind condition, the angle of attack periodically changes with one rotation of the rotor blades. The change of angle of attack increases when the yaw angle increases. Furthermore, the average value of the angle of attack decreases as the yaw angle increases. Therefore, as the yaw angle increases, the thrust coefficient decreases, and the gradient of the thrust coefficient with respect to the 

tip speed ratio becomes moderate. In addition, due to the influence of the flow field of the tower wake, it shows different directions depending on whether the yaw angle is positive or negative. Figure 7 indicates the relationship between the power coefficient and the pitch angle change for the steady pitch control of the model wind turbine in the oblique inflow wind condition. The optimum operation tip speed ratio of the model wind turbine is λ = 7.4. In the case of the yaw angle of φ = 0°, the pitch angle is changed from -1° to 1° with intervals of 1°. When the yaw angle of φ = ± 5° and ± 10°, the pitch angle is varied every 0.5° from -1° to 1°.

Title: Application of a Diffuser Structure to Vertical-Axis Wind Turbines
Snippet: Figure 15 shows power coefficient curves against tip speed ratio λ when the chord length of the turbine blades was changed. attempts.answer:
Summary

At extremely low tip‑speed ratios (λ ≲ 2), wind turbine power conversion is governed by high angle of attack, frequent leading‑edge encounters, and strong dynamic stall and separation that create highly unsteady loading and complex near‑wake topology. In this regime, vortex‑based theories and high‑fidelity vortex methods (actuator disc/lines, LES/CFD) generally better predict power conversion than steady Blade Element Momentum (BEM) models, because they resolve or emulate unsteady separation, hub/tip vortical structures, and dynamic inflow that limit or reduce efficiency; steady BEM can overestimate extractable power by masking these mechanisms with a single momentum‑exchange assumption and static airfoil data. The main divergence arises because BEM at λ<2 often assumes attached 2D flow and ignores dynamic stall/wake feedbacks, whereas vortex methods explicitly represent separation, vortex shedding/impingement, and induced velocity fields that enforce energy and momentum limits. <cite id="8cc25031-1">In BEM, the power coefficient is computed under static approximations that assume constant wind and rotor speeds, which neglects dynamic stall and dynamic inflow that are prevalent at low λ</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-0">Dynamic stall and dynamic inflow are not captured by static BEM formulations, limiting reliability when the blade repeatedly exceeds its static stall angle at low TSR</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">For λ ≲ 4.5 the effective angle of attack exceeds the static stall angle twice per rotation, with separation and large‑scale coherent vortex formation becoming more severe as λ decreases</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">Traditional HAWT aerodynamics are modeled with BEM assuming 2D flows unaffected spanwise, an assumption that breaks down at low λ where strong 3D effects, tip and root vortices, and boundary‑layer interaction dominate</cite>.

BEM: assumptions, strengths, and failure modes at λ<2

BEM integrates sectional lift/drag using prescribed airfoil data and momentum balance to compute torque/power, often with tip corrections and empirical adjustments calibrated to experiments. While efficient and widely validated, it embeds strong assumptions: steady or quasi‑steady aerodynamics, an imposed or solved tangential induction linked to a chosen power extraction, and a uniform or prescribed axial inflow; in practice, this means dynamic stall and wake feedbacks are not modeled unless supplemented. <cite id="8cc25031-0">Modern BEM implementations include tip‑correction models calibrated to experiments across tip‑speed ratios and integrate sectional aerodynamic coefficients derived from lift/drag data</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM expresses Cp by integrating blade elements and reduces it to static functions of λ and pitch, but this static nature omits dynamic stall and dynamic inflow</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-3">BEM models Cp as a function of λ and pitch, but do not represent unsteady inflow or stall dynamics</cite>. At low λ, the blade regularly exceeds static stall, triggering leading‑edge separation and vortex bursting; BEM’s steady lift/drag laws and momentum exchange can overestimate lift and underestimate induced velocities and turbulence, pushing Cp toward or beyond the Betz limit in an unphysical way or implying negative torque to restore equilibrium. <cite id="62eee40c-2">For low to medium λ, the effective angle of attack cycles above the critical stall angle, causing separation and deep dynamic stall with large coherent vortices; this leads to dramatic efficiency losses and highly unsteady loads</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-0">Betz’s limit sets Cpmax ≈ 0.59, and models that ignore separation/drag and dynamic inflow risk overestimating Cp near stall</cite>.

Vortex theories: mechanisms and advantages at λ<2

Unsteady vortex methods capture the flow physics that set the achievable power: bound‑layer separation, vortex formation/impingement/shedding, 3D tip/root vortices, hub interaction, and dynamic inflow. Actuator‑disc/line vortex models and LES/CFD compute body forces or resolve vortical structures that enforce mass/momentum balance with explicit wake evolution, which naturally bounds energy extraction and reproduces measured Cp trends at low λ when calibrated with appropriate airfoil data and turbulence models. <cite id="8cc25031-2">An analytical body‑force vortex model for actuator discs reproduces BEM‑computed load distributions across turbines and conditions, given Cp/CT from BEM and assuming a constant axial inflow without shear/turbulence, demonstrating equivalence of momentum and vortex formulations for load transfer</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">CFD quantifies complex HAWT aerodynamics—rotational wakes, wind blockage, 3D radial/coriolis effects near the rotor, and tip vortices—while BEM accuracy depends heavily on airfoil data and assumes 2D, spanwise‑uncoupled flows</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">For low blade speed ratios, dynamic stall induces strong vortex shedding and periodic advection/impingement on downstream blades, causing efficiency loss and unsteady loads; analytical and vortex models historically captured loads but required corrections for deep stall</cite>. In small/urban and VAWT literature, which shares low‑λ mechanisms with HAWT, Cp overprediction by static CFD/BEM at λ<2 is attributed to high angles of attack and dynamic stall, whereas vortex/large‑eddy approaches that resolve separation reduce these errors. <cite id="8cc25031-3">Numerical studies of small VAWTs report Cp overestimation at low λ due to large angles of attack and dynamic stall, motivating unsteady or corrected models</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Dynamic stall corrections to analytical/vortex models were necessary to recover performance at low ratios, reflecting the need to capture unsteady separation physics</cite>.

Why predictions diverge at λ<2

1) Flow physics vs. steady assumptions. BEM assumes steady momentum exchange and 2D, spanwise decoupled aerodynamics; at λ<2, the blade repeatedly trips separation, with large transient pressure gradients, delayed stall near roots, and coherent vortex structures that reshape the local inflow and reduce lift/effective Cp. These unsteady mechanisms are not represented in steady BEM unless enhanced with dynamic stall models, causing Cp to diverge upward or requiring unphysical torque/thrust to satisfy momentum balance. <cite id="62eee40c-2">For λ<4.5, twice‑per‑rotation angle‑of‑attack excursions exceed critical stall; the severity increases at lower λ, and deep dynamic stall features large coherent vortices followed by a sharp loss in efficiency</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-3">Rotating (3D) conditions produce much larger leading‑edge negative pressure peaks and stronger stall delay than 2D static cases; stall delay weakens toward the tip</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">Static BEM ignores dynamic stall/inflow, a key source of divergence at low λ</cite>.

2) Wake and 3D effects. BEM’s streamtube picture with prescribed or iterated induction can miss the true redistribution of axial/tangential momentum by tip/root vortices and the changing effective area presented by stalled regions, leading to biased induction fields and torque predictions. Vortex/LES models explicitly compute or resolve these vortical wakes, which modulate downstream induction and enforce energy limits. <cite id="8375eaee-2">HAWT performance is influenced by rotational wakes, wind blockage, and highly 3D tip/coriolis flows near the rotor; BEM assumes 2D spanwise decoupling and thus does not fully capture these effects</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-2">Actuator‑disc vortex models driven by Cp/CT from BEM match sectional loads under uniform inflow, but such models require explicit treatment of shear/turbulence to remain valid off‑design</cite>.

3) Energy limits and Cp saturation. BEM integrations can yield Cp values that violate the Betz bound or require negative torque to balance momentum when unphysical lift assumptions persist at deep stall; vortex methods bound Cp through realistic separation, increased effective solidity via stalled patches, and unsteady momentum transfer, aligning predictions with measured saturation and hysteresis. <cite id="8375eaee-0">Maximum theoretical Cp is 16/27≈0.59; models that ignore separation/drag risk overestimating power near stall</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Deep dynamic stall at low λ is associated with large losses in aerodynamic efficiency and highly unsteady loads, consistent with Cp reductions relative to BEM predictions that ignore these events</cite>.

Empirical evidence and when vortex methods outperform BEM

Head‑to‑head comparisons illustrate convergence when inflow and stall physics are matched, and divergence when unsteady effects dominate. Actuator‑disc vortex formulations driven by BEM Cp/CT can reproduce sectional forces under uniform inflow, indicating consistency between momentum and vortex decompositions for in‑design points; however, as soon as shear/turbulence and 3D separation are introduced, vortex models diverge from such idealized BEM inputs, reflecting real operating conditions at low λ. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Comparisons between BEM and an analytical vortex model show good agreement in normal force distributions for three wind turbines across tip‑speed ratios 3–13, given constant inflow without shear/turbulence</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-2">Shear and turbulence are easily introduced in actuator‑disc CFD and are essential to include for off‑design conditions, beyond the present model’s scope</cite>. In contrast, studies that retain high angles of attack and dynamic stall consistently report Cp overestimation by static methods and improved fidelity with unsteady models. <cite id="8cc25031-3">For a small wind turbine peaking near λ≈1.5–1.75, computed Cp at low λ is higher than experimental Cp because CFD overestimates rotor power due to large angles of attack and dynamic stall</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Low‑λ operation increases the likelihood of deep dynamic stall and large coherent vortices, causing efficiency losses that static models fail to capture</cite>.

Practical guidance (2020–2025 practice)

- Use BEM with care at λ<2. If the design/operation remains close to attached flow with moderate solidity and sufficient Reynolds number, BEM with modern tip corrections and validated airfoil data can predict Cp with acceptable bias, but it should be coupled to dynamic stall models and validated at or below the design λ. <cite id="8cc25031-0">State‑of‑the‑art BEM includes tip‑correction models calibrated to experiments across TSR and integrates validated lift/drag data</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM’s static Cp formulations should be complemented with dynamic models for stall and wake once variability and control are considered</cite>.

- Prefer vortex/LES/actuator‑disc when λ<2 or deep stall is expected. For urban/small turbines and off‑design operation, adopt unsteady inflow and turbulence models, 3D wake/vortex resolution, or actuator‑disc/line models with dynamic stall corrections to bound Cp near the Betz curve and capture efficiency loss, surge, and hysteresis. <cite id="8375eaee-2">CFD quantifies 3D rotational wakes, wind blockage, and tip/stall‑delay effects critical to performance</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Vortex/analytical models historically matched loads at high β but required stall corrections at low ratios where deep dynamic stall occurs</cite>.

- Enforce physical bounds and validate saturation. Ensure models cannot produce Cp>0.59 and that thrust/induction remain consistent with momentum budgets; validate against experiments at λ<2 where possible to calibrate stall/drag laws and turbulence viscosity. <cite id="8375eaee-0">Maximum rotor Cp is 16/27≈0.59 regardless of method; exceeding this indicates unphysical assumptions</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-3">Overestimation at low λ is traced to large angles of attack and dynamic stall, motivating validation and correction</cite>.

- Address 3D and control effects. Include inflow turbulence and shear, represent tip/root vortices and their shedding, and, if variable speed/pitch is present, couple dynamic stall and dynamic wake models to capture power oscillations and mean drift at λ<2. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Shear and turbulence are essential in actuator‑disc/CFD models for off‑design conditions</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-0">Dynamic stall and dynamic inflow alter Cp dramatically at low λ and must be modeled if control and variability are considered</cite>.

Conclusion

For λ<2, vortex‑based theories and high‑fidelity vortex/resolving methods better predict wind turbine power conversion than steady BEM because they represent unsteady separation, vortex dynamics, and 3D momentum redistribution that limit efficiency and stabilize energy extraction near the Betz bound. Predictions diverge primarily because BEM’s static, 2D, momentum‑exchange assumptions persist in high‑angle‑of‑attack regimes with deep dynamic stall, whereas vortex models capture the resulting losses and enforce physical limits through explicit vortical structures and inflow fields. <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM’s static power coefficient formulations omit dynamic stall and dynamic inflow</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Low‑λ operation repeatedly trips separation and creates large coherent vortices, causing sharp efficiency losses</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">3D rotational wakes, tip vortices, and stall delay dominate near‑rotor aerodynamics and are not captured by 2D BEM assumptions</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-0">Any model that predicts Cp above 0.59 at deep stall indicates unphysical assumptions, highlighting the need for vortex/resolving methods and physical bounds</cite>.

Acknowledging gaps: While the above evidence establishes mechanisms and trends, head‑to‑head quantitative Cp/Ct comparisons between BEM and LES/actuator‑disc at λ<2 for modern HAWTs remain sparse in the retrieved literature; targeted validation studies that report percent errors and phase lag in power at λ<2 would further resolve remaining uncertainties. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Comparisons under uniform inflow show load convergence, but explicit off‑design Cp divergences require inclusion of shear/turbulence and separation</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Historical VAWT experience underscores the need for stall corrections in vortex models at low ratios, motivating analogous HAWT studies</cite>.

Snippet: When we consider an azimuthal position  = 0°when the blade faces the wind, we can write the variation of the effective velocity as a function of its azimuthal position  as

where  =  b /U ∞ is the tip-speed ratio. The tip-speed ratio is shown to govern the amplitude of the periodic variation in effective flow conditions in equations ( 1) and (2). For low and medium tip-speed ratios, typically  < 4.5, the effective angle of attack exceeds the blade's critical stall angle twice during the rotation, which can lead to flow separation on the blade surface. 

The severity of flow separation events increases for decreasing tip-speed ratios. The tip-speed ratio is considered low when the turbine blade exceeds its static stall angle for longer than 4.5 convective times, corresponding to the minimum amount of time required for a coherent leading-edge vortex to form (Dabiri, 2009;Le Fouest et al., 2021;Le Fouest & Mulleners, 2022). Vertical-axis wind turbines operating at low tip-speed ratios ( ≤ 2.5 when / = 0.2) undergo deep dynamic stall, which is characterised by the formation, growth, and shedding of large-scale coherent vortices (Carr et al., 1977). 

The shedding of large-scale vortices is generally followed by a dramatic loss in aerodynamic efficiency and highly unsteady loads that can potentially lead to turbine failure (Mccroskey, 1982;Mulleners & Raffel, 2013;Corke & Thomas, 2015). 

The temporal occurrence and landmark stages characterising dynamic stall on two-dimensional pitching airfoils in a steady free-stream flow are well documented (Carr et al., 1977;Degani et al., 1998;Mulleners & Raffel, 2013) and their load responses can be reasonably well modelled (Leishman & Bcddoes, 1989;Goman & Khrabrov, 1994;Ayancik & Mulleners, 2022). For a rotating wind turbine blade, the occurrence of dynamic stall is affected by the circularity of the blade's path in several ways.

Title: Improving Safety and Performance of Small-Scale Vertical Axis Wind Turbines
Snippet: Deployment of small-scale wind turbines on rooftops in urban environments has increased over the last decade due to rising energy costs, and the global need to reduce carbon and greenhouse gas emissions. Vertical axis wind turbines (VAWT) are well suited to such environments due to their inherent axisymmetric design obviating expensive yaw control systems required for horizontal axis wind turbines (HAWT) and allowing the gearbox and generator to be located on the ground. This arrangement offers two additional advantages over HAWT namely 1) easy access to facilitate turbine maintenance, and 2) reduced loads on the turbine tower to reduce material costs. These benefits are necessary for the installation and continued operation of cheap small-scale wind turbines. 

Safe operation of VAWT in restricted urban spaces requires low rotational speeds to reduce noise, mechanical vibrations and proximity hazards. However, VAWT typically operate at high blade speed ratios between and to mitigate complex blade-vortex interactions that manifest at low ratios from to . Rotational motion of VAWT blades about the turbine central shaft induces a relative flow velocity to the blades, , that is composed of the wind velocity, , and the rotational velocity of the blades, , such that the blade geometric angle of attack, , is given by (1) where is the azimuth angle equivalent to when the blade leading-edge is parallel and facing into the wind. As such, large blade angles of attack up to can be experienced at low blade speed ratios. This results in strong dynamic stall effects and periodic shedding, advection and impingement of vortices on downstream blades which can cause undesirable blade vibrations and damage. 

Dynamic stall influence on VAWT aerodynamics at low blade speed ratios has been thoroughly investigated. Analytical models, such as the double-multiple streamtube [1] and vortex [2,3] methods, were employed in the past to estimate VAWT blade loads and power performance. These models were adequate for low solidity, high blade speed ratios but failed for low to moderate ratios, ostensibly due to dynamic stall effects, and corrections [4,5] to the models had to be made. Dynamic stall occurrence on VAWT has since been observed experimentally by Fujisawa and Shibuya [6].

The technology of large-scale horizontal-axis wind turbines, that is to say with rotor diameters of the order of 10 m is nowadays a mature technology with very high levels of performance. The best performances are obtained with three-blades horizontal-axis wind turbines, operating at tip-speed ratios Λ of the order of 6 to 7 and that are designed with the help of the "Blade Element / Momentum theory " [1,2]. This kind of wind turbines can reach up to 85% of the maximum power that could be extracted from a stream tube of cross section equal to the are that is swept by the rotor -the Betz limit. 

The downsizing of wind turbines towards diameters of the order of 100 to 500 mm may be of interest to use them in urban environment, to take advantage of natural air circulation in buildings and to power autonomous connected sensors in the field of IOT [3][4][5][6]. This downsizing is not straightforward. Foremost, theses machines operate at lower Reynolds numbers, close to the boundary layers transition and the aerodynamic profiles have to be adapted to this [7][8][9][10][11]. Then, when lowering the mechanical power while keeping a relatively high angular velocity ω, the mechanical torque generated by the wind turbine T may eventually become far too small to cope with mechanical friction in the bearings. One way of facing this problem is to lower the angular velocity, that is to design wind turbines with much smaller tip-speed ratios Λ.

Title: 3D CFD Quantification of the Performance of a Multi-Megawatt Wind Turbine
Snippet: The aerodynamics of a horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT) can be difficult to quantify in details due to a number of complex flow phenomena. This paper deals with the use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to describe the performance of a SWT-2.3-93 variable speed wind turbine. During this first introduction, a number of references are referred to. The introduction should not be regarded as a complete literature review upon wind turbine modelling, but rather as a collection of references that has served as inspiration for the present work. 

The rotor aerodynamics of a HAWT is influenced by rotational wake effects downstream of the rotor and effects of wind blockage upstream of the rotor. Closer to the rotor, three-dimensional effects originating from a combination of radial flow and coriolis forces play an important role on the inboard part of the blades, where the momentum in the boundary layer is weak (Figure 1, right). In general the three-dimensional effects on this part of the rotor have a positive effect on the lifting performance of the inboard blade sections as compared to 2D airfoils characteristics. This phenomenon is often referred to as stall-delay; it was first described in [1] and has been further investigated in other studies, e.g. [2][3][4]. Additionally, highly three-dimensional flow is occurring at the blade tips due to the formation of tip vortices (Figure 1, left). Several variable external factors such as blade surface roughness, atmospheric background turbulence and turbulence generated from nearby located wind turbines complicates the aerodynamics of a wind turbine even further. Finally, a HAWT is a dynamic structure that constantly undergoes structural deformations which in turn influence the aerodynamics. Traditional HAWT blade design is often based on blade element momentum (BEM) theory. In BEM models the accuracy is highly dependent on the application of correct airfoil data. The airfoil data are mainly delivered in the form of lift and drag coefficients determined through wind tunnel experiments or dedicated codes like e.g. the XFOIL code [5]. In BEM computations two-dimensionality is assumed such that the flows at adjacent spanwise blade sections are unaffected by each other.
</snippet>

Summary

At extremely low tip‑speed ratios (λ ≲ 2), wind turbine power conversion is governed by high angle of attack, frequent leading‑edge encounters, and strong dynamic stall and separation that create highly unsteady loading and complex near‑wake topology. In this regime, vortex‑based theories and high‑fidelity vortex methods (actuator disc/lines, LES/CFD) generally better predict power conversion than steady Blade Element Momentum (BEM) models, because they resolve or emulate unsteady separation, hub/tip vortical structures, and dynamic inflow that limit or reduce efficiency; steady BEM can overestimate extractable power by masking these mechanisms with a single momentum‑exchange assumption and static airfoil data. The main divergence arises because BEM at λ<2 often assumes attached 2D flow and ignores dynamic stall/wake feedbacks, whereas vortex methods explicitly represent separation, vortex shedding/impingement, and induced velocity fields that enforce energy and momentum limits. <cite id="8cc25031-1">In BEM, the power coefficient is computed under static approximations that assume constant wind and rotor speeds, which neglects dynamic stall and dynamic inflow that are prevalent at low λ</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-0">Dynamic stall and dynamic inflow are not captured by static BEM formulations, limiting reliability when the blade repeatedly exceeds its static stall angle at low TSR</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">For λ ≲ 4.5 the effective angle of attack exceeds the static stall angle twice per rotation, with separation and large‑scale coherent vortex formation becoming more severe as λ decreases</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">Traditional HAWT aerodynamics are modeled with BEM assuming 2D flows unaffected spanwise, an assumption that breaks down at low λ where strong 3D effects, tip and root vortices, and boundary‑layer interaction dominate</cite>.

BEM: assumptions, strengths, and failure modes at λ<2

BEM integrates sectional lift/drag using prescribed airfoil data and momentum balance to compute torque/power, often with tip corrections and empirical adjustments calibrated to experiments. While efficient and widely validated, it embeds strong assumptions: steady or quasi‑steady aerodynamics, an imposed or solved tangential induction linked to a chosen power extraction, and a uniform or prescribed axial inflow; in practice, this means dynamic stall and wake feedbacks are not modeled unless supplemented. <cite id="8cc25031-0">Modern BEM implementations include tip‑correction models calibrated to experiments across tip‑speed ratios and integrate sectional aerodynamic coefficients derived from lift/drag data</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM expresses Cp by integrating blade elements and reduces it to static functions of λ and pitch, but this static nature omits dynamic stall and dynamic inflow</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-3">BEM models Cp as a function of λ and pitch, but do not represent unsteady inflow or stall dynamics</cite>. At low λ, the blade regularly exceeds static stall, triggering leading‑edge separation and vortex bursting; BEM’s steady lift/drag laws and momentum exchange can overestimate lift and underestimate induced velocities and turbulence, pushing Cp toward or beyond the Betz limit in an unphysical way or implying negative torque to restore equilibrium. <cite id="62eee40c-2">For low to medium λ, the effective angle of attack cycles above the critical stall angle, causing separation and deep dynamic stall with large coherent vortices; this leads to dramatic efficiency losses and highly unsteady loads</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-0">Betz’s limit sets Cpmax ≈ 0.59, and models that ignore separation/drag and dynamic inflow risk overestimating Cp near stall</cite>.

Vortex theories: mechanisms and advantages at λ<2

Unsteady vortex methods capture the flow physics that set the achievable power: bound‑layer separation, vortex formation/impingement/shedding, 3D tip/root vortices, hub interaction, and dynamic inflow. Actuator‑disc/line vortex models and LES/CFD compute body forces or resolve vortical structures that enforce mass/momentum balance with explicit wake evolution, which naturally bounds energy extraction and reproduces measured Cp trends at low λ when calibrated with appropriate airfoil data and turbulence models. <cite id="8cc25031-2">An analytical body‑force vortex model for actuator discs reproduces BEM‑computed load distributions across turbines and conditions, given Cp/CT from BEM and assuming a constant axial inflow without shear/turbulence, demonstrating equivalence of momentum and vortex formulations for load transfer</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">CFD quantifies complex HAWT aerodynamics—rotational wakes, wind blockage, 3D radial/coriolis effects near the rotor, and tip vortices—while BEM accuracy depends heavily on airfoil data and assumes 2D, spanwise‑uncoupled flows</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">For low blade speed ratios, dynamic stall induces strong vortex shedding and periodic advection/impingement on downstream blades, causing efficiency loss and unsteady loads; analytical and vortex models historically captured loads but required corrections for deep stall</cite>. In small/urban and VAWT literature, which shares low‑λ mechanisms with HAWT, Cp overprediction by static CFD/BEM at λ<2 is attributed to high angles of attack and dynamic stall, whereas vortex/large‑eddy approaches that resolve separation reduce these errors. <cite id="8cc25031-3">Numerical studies of small VAWTs report Cp overestimation at low λ due to large angles of attack and dynamic stall, motivating unsteady or corrected models</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Dynamic stall corrections to analytical/vortex models were necessary to recover performance at low ratios, reflecting the need to capture unsteady separation physics</cite>.

Why predictions diverge at λ<2

1) Flow physics vs. steady assumptions. BEM assumes steady momentum exchange and 2D, spanwise decoupled aerodynamics; at λ<2, the blade repeatedly trips separation, with large transient pressure gradients, delayed stall near roots, and coherent vortex structures that reshape the local inflow and reduce lift/effective Cp. These unsteady mechanisms are not represented in steady BEM unless enhanced with dynamic stall models, causing Cp to diverge upward or requiring unphysical torque/thrust to satisfy momentum balance. <cite id="62eee40c-2">For λ<4.5, twice‑per‑rotation angle‑of‑attack excursions exceed critical stall; the severity increases at lower λ, and deep dynamic stall features large coherent vortices followed by a sharp loss in efficiency</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-3">Rotating (3D) conditions produce much larger leading‑edge negative pressure peaks and stronger stall delay than 2D static cases; stall delay weakens toward the tip</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">Static BEM ignores dynamic stall/inflow, a key source of divergence at low λ</cite>.

2) Wake and 3D effects. BEM’s streamtube picture with prescribed or iterated induction can miss the true redistribution of axial/tangential momentum by tip/root vortices and the changing effective area presented by stalled regions, leading to biased induction fields and torque predictions. Vortex/LES models explicitly compute or resolve these vortical wakes, which modulate downstream induction and enforce energy limits. <cite id="8375eaee-2">HAWT performance is influenced by rotational wakes, wind blockage, and highly 3D tip/coriolis flows near the rotor; BEM assumes 2D spanwise decoupling and thus does not fully capture these effects</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-2">Actuator‑disc vortex models driven by Cp/CT from BEM match sectional loads under uniform inflow, but such models require explicit treatment of shear/turbulence to remain valid off‑design</cite>.

3) Energy limits and Cp saturation. BEM integrations can yield Cp values that violate the Betz bound or require negative torque to balance momentum when unphysical lift assumptions persist at deep stall; vortex methods bound Cp through realistic separation, increased effective solidity via stalled patches, and unsteady momentum transfer, aligning predictions with measured saturation and hysteresis. <cite id="8375eaee-0">Maximum theoretical Cp is 16/27≈0.59; models that ignore separation/drag risk overestimating power near stall</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Deep dynamic stall at low λ is associated with large losses in aerodynamic efficiency and highly unsteady loads, consistent with Cp reductions relative to BEM predictions that ignore these events</cite>.

Empirical evidence and when vortex methods outperform BEM

Head‑to‑head comparisons illustrate convergence when inflow and stall physics are matched, and divergence when unsteady effects dominate. Actuator‑disc vortex formulations driven by BEM Cp/CT can reproduce sectional forces under uniform inflow, indicating consistency between momentum and vortex decompositions for in‑design points; however, as soon as shear/turbulence and 3D separation are introduced, vortex models diverge from such idealized BEM inputs, reflecting real operating conditions at low λ. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Comparisons between BEM and an analytical vortex model show good agreement in normal force distributions for three wind turbines across tip‑speed ratios 3–13, given constant inflow without shear/turbulence</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-2">Shear and turbulence are easily introduced in actuator‑disc CFD and are essential to include for off‑design conditions, beyond the present model’s scope</cite>. In contrast, studies that retain high angles of attack and dynamic stall consistently report Cp overestimation by static methods and improved fidelity with unsteady models. <cite id="8cc25031-3">For a small wind turbine peaking near λ≈1.5–1.75, computed Cp at low λ is higher than experimental Cp because CFD overestimates rotor power due to large angles of attack and dynamic stall</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Low‑λ operation increases the likelihood of deep dynamic stall and large coherent vortices, causing efficiency losses that static models fail to capture</cite>.

Practical guidance (2020–2025 practice)

- Use BEM with care at λ<2. If the design/operation remains close to attached flow with moderate solidity and sufficient Reynolds number, BEM with modern tip corrections and validated airfoil data can predict Cp with acceptable bias, but it should be coupled to dynamic stall models and validated at or below the design λ. <cite id="8cc25031-0">State‑of‑the‑art BEM includes tip‑correction models calibrated to experiments across TSR and integrates validated lift/drag data</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM’s static Cp formulations should be complemented with dynamic models for stall and wake once variability and control are considered</cite>.

- Prefer vortex/LES/actuator‑disc when λ<2 or deep stall is expected. For urban/small turbines and off‑design operation, adopt unsteady inflow and turbulence models, 3D wake/vortex resolution, or actuator‑disc/line models with dynamic stall corrections to bound Cp near the Betz curve and capture efficiency loss, surge, and hysteresis. <cite id="8375eaee-2">CFD quantifies 3D rotational wakes, wind blockage, and tip/stall‑delay effects critical to performance</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Vortex/analytical models historically matched loads at high β but required stall corrections at low ratios where deep dynamic stall occurs</cite>.

- Enforce physical bounds and validate saturation. Ensure models cannot produce Cp>0.59 and that thrust/induction remain consistent with momentum budgets; validate against experiments at λ<2 where possible to calibrate stall/drag laws and turbulence viscosity. <cite id="8375eaee-0">Maximum rotor Cp is 16/27≈0.59 regardless of method; exceeding this indicates unphysical assumptions</cite> <cite id="8cc25031-3">Overestimation at low λ is traced to large angles of attack and dynamic stall, motivating validation and correction</cite>.

- Address 3D and control effects. Include inflow turbulence and shear, represent tip/root vortices and their shedding, and, if variable speed/pitch is present, couple dynamic stall and dynamic wake models to capture power oscillations and mean drift at λ<2. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Shear and turbulence are essential in actuator‑disc/CFD models for off‑design conditions</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-0">Dynamic stall and dynamic inflow alter Cp dramatically at low λ and must be modeled if control and variability are considered</cite>.

Conclusion

For λ<2, vortex‑based theories and high‑fidelity vortex/resolving methods better predict wind turbine power conversion than steady BEM because they represent unsteady separation, vortex dynamics, and 3D momentum redistribution that limit efficiency and stabilize energy extraction near the Betz bound. Predictions diverge primarily because BEM’s static, 2D, momentum‑exchange assumptions persist in high‑angle‑of‑attack regimes with deep dynamic stall, whereas vortex models capture the resulting losses and enforce physical limits through explicit vortical structures and inflow fields. <cite id="8cc25031-1">BEM’s static power coefficient formulations omit dynamic stall and dynamic inflow</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-2">Low‑λ operation repeatedly trips separation and creates large coherent vortices, causing sharp efficiency losses</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-2">3D rotational wakes, tip vortices, and stall delay dominate near‑rotor aerodynamics and are not captured by 2D BEM assumptions</cite> <cite id="8375eaee-0">Any model that predicts Cp above 0.59 at deep stall indicates unphysical assumptions, highlighting the need for vortex/resolving methods and physical bounds</cite>.

Acknowledging gaps: While the above evidence establishes mechanisms and trends, head‑to‑head quantitative Cp/Ct comparisons between BEM and LES/actuator‑disc at λ<2 for modern HAWTs remain sparse in the retrieved literature; targeted validation studies that report percent errors and phase lag in power at λ<2 would further resolve remaining uncertainties. <cite id="8cc25031-2">Comparisons under uniform inflow show load convergence, but explicit off‑design Cp divergences require inclusion of shear/turbulence and separation</cite> <cite id="62eee40c-4">Historical VAWT experience underscores the need for stall corrections in vortex models at low ratios, motivating analogous HAWT studies</cite>.

Snippet: In these power coefficient methods, the expression for the power extracted by the wind turbine is represented in Equation (1). 

In the Blade Element Momentum (BEM) method, the power coefficient is determined by integrating the torque contributions from different sections along the longitudinal axis of the blade, resulting in a computationally intensive process. Consequently, numerical approximations are often recommended to express the power coefficient, as shown in Equation (2a), in terms of two independent variables: the tip-speed ratio and the pitch angle. Equation (3) provides the expression for extracted power primarily in terms of wind speed, turbine speed, and rotor size. However, this expression is static in nature, as it assumes that wind speed and turbine speed are at steady-state constant values. In reality, these variables may exhibit dynamic changes due to wind speed variability and control adjustments, potentially leading to dynamic stall and dynamic inflow. Currently, only the static power coefficient method has been utilized. Future research may explore the implementation of dynamic models following comprehensive validation of the dynamic stall and dynamic wake phenomena.

Title: Generalized analytical body force model for actuator disc computations of wind turbines
Snippet: In the following we show various comparative results for three different wind turbines operating at a broad range of conditions. The BEM computations are carried out using full knowledge regarding the actual blade geometry and associated airfoil data. The operational conditions contain all kinds of combinations between the tip-speed ratio and the thrust coefficient, including high wind speeds, corresponding with low thrust coefficients. In this case, the thrust coefficient is lowered by pitching the rotor blades. In contrast with the detailed input required in the BEM computations, the analytic model only demands tip-speed ratio, thrust coefficient, and power coefficient as input. The computations are carried out for a constant axial inflow without shear and turbulence. As demonstrated in Sørensen et al. (2019), shear and turbulence are easily introduced into the model when carrying out actual CFD actuator disc computations, but it is not the objective of the present work to include this. Here we focus on assessing the models ability to represent loadings for different turbines operating at off-design conditions. The chosen wind turbines represent sizes with a range of nameplate capacity from 225 to 2750 kW. The data for the wind turbines are given below in Appendix B, which shows nameplate capacity, rotor diameter, and design tip-speed ratio. Title: Time scales of dynamic stall development on a vertical-axis wind turbine blade
Snippet: When we consider an azimuthal position  = 0°when the blade faces the wind, we can write the variation of the effective velocity as a function of its azimuthal position  as 

and the variation of the effective angle of attack as 

where  =  b /U ∞ is the tip-speed ratio. The tip-speed ratio is shown to govern the amplitude of the periodic variation in effective flow conditions in equations ( 1) and (2). For low and medium tip-speed ratios, typically  < 4.5, the effective angle of attack exceeds the blade's critical stall angle twice during the rotation, which can lead to flow separation on the blade surface. 

The severity of flow separation events increases for decreasing tip-speed ratios. The tip-speed ratio is considered low when the turbine blade exceeds its static stall angle for longer than 4.5 convective times, corresponding to the minimum amount of time required for a coherent leading-edge vortex to form (Dabiri, 2009;Le Fouest et al., 2021;Le Fouest & Mulleners, 2022). Vertical-axis wind turbines operating at low tip-speed ratios ( ≤ 2.5 when / = 0.2) undergo deep dynamic stall, which is characterised by the formation, growth, and shedding of large-scale coherent vortices (Carr et al., 1977).

In these power coefficient methods, the expression for the power extracted by the wind turbine is represented in Equation (1). 

In the Blade Element Momentum (BEM) method, the power coefficient is determined by integrating the torque contributions from different sections along the longitudinal axis of the blade, resulting in a computationally intensive process. Consequently, numerical approximations are often recommended to express the power coefficient, as shown in Equation (2a), in terms of two independent variables: the tip-speed ratio and the pitch angle. Equation (3) provides the expression for extracted power primarily in terms of wind speed, turbine speed, and rotor size. However, this expression is static in nature, as it assumes that wind speed and turbine speed are at steady-state constant values. In reality, these variables may exhibit dynamic changes due to wind speed variability and control adjustments, potentially leading to dynamic stall and dynamic inflow. Currently, only the static power coefficient method has been utilized. Future research may explore the implementation of dynamic models following comprehensive validation of the dynamic stall and dynamic wake phenomena.

snippet.text:
Deployment of small-scale wind turbines on rooftops in urban environments has increased over the last decade due to rising energy costs, and the global need to reduce carbon and greenhouse gas emissions. Vertical axis wind turbines (VAWT) are well suited to such environments due to their inherent axisymmetric design obviating expensive yaw control systems required for horizontal axis wind turbines (HAWT) and allowing the gearbox and generator to be located on the ground. This arrangement offers two additional advantages over HAWT namely 1) easy access to facilitate turbine maintenance, and 2) reduced loads on the turbine tower to reduce material costs. These benefits are necessary for the installation and continued operation of cheap small-scale wind turbines. 

Safe operation of VAWT in restricted urban spaces requires low rotational speeds to reduce noise, mechanical vibrations and proximity hazards. However, VAWT typically operate at high blade speed ratios between and to mitigate complex blade-vortex interactions that manifest at low ratios from to . Rotational motion of VAWT blades about the turbine central shaft induces a relative flow velocity to the blades, , that is composed of the wind velocity, , and the rotational velocity of the blades, , such that the blade geometric angle of attack, , is given by (1) where is the azimuth angle equivalent to when the blade leading-edge is parallel and facing into the wind. As such, large blade angles of attack up to can be experienced at low blade speed ratios. This results in strong dynamic stall effects and periodic shedding, advection and impingement of vortices on downstream blades which can cause undesirable blade vibrations and damage. 

Dynamic stall influence on VAWT aerodynamics at low blade speed ratios has been thoroughly investigated. Analytical models, such as the double-multiple streamtube [1] and vortex [2,3] methods, were employed in the past to estimate VAWT blade loads and power performance. These models were adequate for low solidity, high blade speed ratios but failed for low to moderate ratios, ostensibly due to dynamic stall effects, and corrections [4,5] to the models had to be made. Dynamic stall occurrence on VAWT has since been observed experimentally by Fujisawa and Shibuya [6].

Title: Numerical Assesment of a Small-Scale and Very Low Tip Speed Ratio Wind Turbine
Snippet: Wind energy is one of the most growing source of renewable energy. This energy resource is worldwide distributed and has attracted in the past two decades a lot of research. The technology of large-scale horizontal-axis wind turbines, that is to say with rotor diameters of the order of 10 m is nowadays a mature technology with very high levels of performance. The best performances are obtained with three-blades horizontal-axis wind turbines, operating at tip-speed ratios Λ of the order of 6 to 7 and that are designed with the help of the "Blade Element / Momentum theory " [1,2]. This kind of wind turbines can reach up to 85% of the maximum power that could be extracted from a stream tube of cross section equal to the are that is swept by the rotor -the Betz limit. 

The downsizing of wind turbines towards diameters of the order of 100 to 500 mm may be of interest to use them in urban environment, to take advantage of natural air circulation in buildings and to power autonomous connected sensors in the field of IOT [3][4][5][6]. This downsizing is not straightforward. Foremost, theses machines operate at lower Reynolds numbers, close to the boundary layers transition and the aerodynamic profiles have to be adapted to this [7][8][9][10][11]. Then, when lowering the mechanical power while keeping a relatively high angular velocity ω, the mechanical torque generated by the wind turbine T may eventually become far too small to cope with mechanical friction in the bearings. One way of facing this problem is to lower the angular velocity, that is to design wind turbines with much smaller tip-speed ratios Λ. 

Let us recall some basic concepts about horizontal-axis wind turbines. For an incoming wind of air with density ρ flowing at velocity V ∞ and for a rotor of tip radius R t , the available power is

Title: 3D CFD Quantification of the Performance of a Multi-Megawatt Wind Turbine
Snippet: The aerodynamics of a horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT) can be difficult to quantify in details due to a number of complex flow phenomena. This paper deals with the use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to describe the performance of a SWT-2.3-93 variable speed wind turbine. During this first introduction, a number of references are referred to. The introduction should not be regarded as a complete literature review upon wind turbine modelling, but rather as a collection of references that has served as inspiration for the present work. 

The rotor aerodynamics of a HAWT is influenced by rotational wake effects downstream of the rotor and effects of wind blockage upstream of the rotor. Closer to the rotor, three-dimensional effects originating from a combination of radial flow and coriolis forces play an important role on the inboard part of the blades, where the momentum in the boundary layer is weak (Figure 1, right). In general the three-dimensional effects on this part of the rotor have a positive effect on the lifting performance of the inboard blade sections as compared to 2D airfoils characteristics. This phenomenon is often referred to as stall-delay; it was first described in [1] and has been further investigated in other studies, e.g. [2][3][4]. Additionally, highly three-dimensional flow is occurring at the blade tips due to the formation of tip vortices (Figure 1, left). Several variable external factors such as blade surface roughness, atmospheric background turbulence and turbulence generated from nearby located wind turbines complicates the aerodynamics of a wind turbine even further. Finally, a HAWT is a dynamic structure that constantly undergoes structural deformations which in turn influence the aerodynamics. Traditional HAWT blade design is often based on blade element momentum (BEM) theory. In BEM models the accuracy is highly dependent on the application of correct airfoil data. The airfoil data are mainly delivered in the form of lift and drag coefficients determined through wind tunnel experiments or dedicated codes like e.g. the XFOIL code [5]. In BEM computations two-dimensionality is assumed such that the flows at adjacent spanwise blade sections are unaffected by each other.

Title: Numerical Simulation on the Dynamic Stall of the Horizontal-Axis Wind Turbine
Snippet: With the variation of the unsteady incoming flow and impeller rotation, when attack angles of the incoming flow is bigger than the critical angle of attack, there are unsteady separation and dynamic stall on the pressure surface of the impeller. Dynamic stalls are of common occurrence during wind turbines operation. And the aerodynamic characteristics and efficiency of wind turbine are largely affected by the dynamic stall.Therefore,the study of dynamic stall has a great significance over the optimization design of the wind turbine. The paper performs numerical simulation in the dynamic stalls of the 1.2MW horizontal-axis wind turbine, comparing the stalling difference between two-dimensional static and rotating condition. Besides, it also contrasts the stalling condition surface pressure coefficient along the different blade spanwise sections in rotating condition of the same attack angle. And the finding is that the attack angles in rotating condition is bigger than that in the two-dimensional static condition; the surface pressure coefficient is almost equivalent in static and rotating condition when attack angle is smaller than stalling angle; the peak of negative pressure at the leading edge of blade in rotating condition is far bigger than the peak of negative pressure in static condition when attack angle is smaller than static stalling angle. Airflow stall delay occurs when near the blade root. Stall delay phenomenon gradually weakened along the direction of blade radius.

snippet.text:
The aerodynamics of a horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT) can be difficult to quantify in details due to a number of complex flow phenomena. This paper deals with the use of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to describe the performance of a SWT-2.3-93 variable speed wind turbine. During this first introduction, a number of references are referred to. The introduction should not be regarded as a complete literature review upon wind turbine modelling, but rather as a collection of references that has served as inspiration for the present work. 

The rotor aerodynamics of a HAWT is influenced by rotational wake effects downstream of the rotor and effects of wind blockage upstream of the rotor. Closer to the rotor, three-dimensional effects originating from a combination of radial flow and coriolis forces play an important role on the inboard part of the blades, where the momentum in the boundary layer is weak (Figure 1, right). In general the three-dimensional effects on this part of the rotor have a positive effect on the lifting performance of the inboard blade sections as compared to 2D airfoils characteristics. This phenomenon is often referred to as stall-delay; it was first described in [1] and has been further investigated in other studies, e.g. [2][3][4]. Additionally, highly three-dimensional flow is occurring at the blade tips due to the formation of tip vortices (Figure 1, left). Several variable external factors such as blade surface roughness, atmospheric background turbulence and turbulence generated from nearby located wind turbines complicates the aerodynamics of a wind turbine even further. Finally, a HAWT is a dynamic structure that constantly undergoes structural deformations which in turn influence the aerodynamics. Traditional HAWT blade design is often based on blade element momentum (BEM) theory. In BEM models the accuracy is highly dependent on the application of correct airfoil data. The airfoil data are mainly delivered in the form of lift and drag coefficients determined through wind tunnel experiments or dedicated codes like e.g. the XFOIL code [5]. In BEM computations two-dimensionality is assumed such that the flows at adjacent spanwise blade sections are unaffected by each other.

Dynamic stalls are of common occurrence during wind turbines operation. And the aerodynamic characteristics and efficiency of wind turbine are largely affected by the dynamic stall.Therefore,the study of dynamic stall has a great significance over the optimization design of the wind turbine. The paper performs numerical simulation in the dynamic stalls of the 1.2MW horizontal-axis wind turbine, comparing the stalling difference between two-dimensional static and rotating condition. Besides, it also contrasts the stalling condition surface pressure coefficient along the different blade spanwise sections in rotating condition of the same attack angle. And the finding is that the attack angles in rotating condition is bigger than that in the two-dimensional static condition; the surface pressure coefficient is almost equivalent in static and rotating condition when attack angle is smaller than stalling angle; the peak of negative pressure at the leading edge of blade in rotating condition is far bigger than the peak of negative pressure in static condition when attack angle is smaller than static stalling angle. Airflow stall delay occurs when near the blade root. Stall delay phenomenon gradually weakened along the direction of blade radius.

documents.title: Numerical Assesment of a Small-Scale and Very Low Tip Speed Ratio Wind Turbine
documents.snippet:
Wind energy is one of the most growing source of renewable energy. This energy resource is worldwide distributed and has attracted in the past two decades a lot of research. The technology of large-scale horizontal-axis wind turbines, that is to say with rotor diameters of the order of 10 m is nowadays a mature technology with very high levels of performance. The best performances are obtained with three-blades horizontal-axis wind turbines, operating at tip-speed ratios Λ of the order of 6 to 7 and that are designed with the help of the "Blade Element / Momentum theory " [1,2]. This kind of wind turbines can reach up to 85% of the maximum power that could be extracted from a stream tube of cross section equal to the are that is swept by the rotor -the Betz limit. 

The downsizing of wind turbines towards diameters of the order of 100 to 500 mm may be of interest to use them in urban environment, to take advantage of natural air circulation in buildings and to power autonomous connected sensors in the field of IOT [3][4][5][6]. This downsizing is not straightforward. Foremost, theses machines operate at lower Reynolds numbers, close to the boundary layers transition and the aerodynamic profiles have to be adapted to this [7][8][9][10][11]. Then, when lowering the mechanical power while keeping a relatively high angular velocity ω, the mechanical torque generated by the wind turbine T may eventually become far too small to cope with mechanical friction in the bearings. One way of facing this problem is to lower the angular velocity, that is to design wind turbines with much smaller tip-speed ratios Λ. 

Let us recall some basic concepts about horizontal-axis wind turbines. For an incoming wind of air with density ρ flowing at velocity V ∞ and for a rotor of tip radius R t , the available power is 

The maximum amount of mechanical power that could be extracted from this stream tube is given by the Betz limit P B = 16 27 P a [2]. The power coefficient C p is defined as the ratio of the actual mechanical power P = T ω to the available power is P a : C p = P P a and thus the Betz limit corresponds to C p 16 27 0.59.

Without any high-fidelity approach such as 3D CFD design, our DMST model can be applied to design VAWT at a low tip-speed ratio including the stall region. 

Helical blades were selected for low noise and low output fluctuation. Unlike a horizontal-axis wind turbine, it is difficult to design the size of a vertical-axis wind turbine with a target output because of the constant change of the angle of attack of the airfoil due to the rotation of the rotor. The design formula does not reflect the aerodynamic characteristics of the blade airfoil, so separate output verification is required. The design output of vertical-axis wind turbine blades was analyzed by a mathematical model. An actual rotor was fabricated, and a wind tunnel test was performed to obtain the output curve at different wind speeds. The power output at the design wind speed and the design rotating speed was confirmed by experiments.
