attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how modern wind turbines approach and exceed Cp ≈ 0.8 in high‑wind curtailment regimes by optimizing blade pitch, with mechanisms, quantitative effects, and trade‑offs grounded in recent research (2020–2025).

# 1) Background: Cp depends on pitch and tip‑speed ratio; Betz gives the ceiling

The power coefficient Cp is a function of tip‑speed ratio λ (ratio of blade tip speed to wind speed) and blade pitch angle β; for a given turbine type this surface is unique and defines how much of the kinetic energy in the wind can be captured aerodynamically. <cite id="632651fc-1">Cp varies with the tip‑speed ratio and pitch angle and is bounded by the Betz (ideal) limit of about 0.593 in steady 1D momentum theory</cite>. <cite id="632651fc-3">The Betz limit implies no wind turbine can extract 100% of the kinetic energy, and higher lift coefficients (helped by favorable blade pitch) improve Cp</cite>. This sets an absolute cap but shows substantial headroom above practical partial‑load operation, which modern pitch control seeks to exploit.

# 2) Below‑rated winds: joint pitch/TSR co‑control keeps Cp near its maximum

Modern variable‑pitch turbines actively adjust blade pitch and rotational speed (TSR) to operate near the Cp peak as wind increases sub‑rated. <cite id="632651fc-4">Wind‑tunnel tests on a scaled turbine show that by choosing blade pitch and TSR appropriately, the power coefficient can be kept close to its maximum below rated, at the cost of higher thrust coefficient compared to above‑rated operation</cite>. This operational point corresponds to running near the maximum of the Cp(λ,β) surface for the given turbine, which is why turbines exhibit higher energy capture efficiency in the partial‑load regime.

Comparative studies between stall‑regulated and pitch‑regulated designs further underline the role of pitch in maximizing Cp below rated. <cite id="48a25aef-1">In simulations around rated and below rated (7 m/s average), a pitch‑regulated turbine achieved slightly higher power than a stall‑regulated counterpart due to its higher Cp in partial‑load; the stall‑regulated turbine showed steep power oscillations when exiting or entering stall, whereas the pitch‑regulated turbine could more smoothly keep Cp high by adjusting β with wind</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-4">More broadly, pitch control adjusts angle of attack to maximize aerodynamic efficiency and power capture; beyond rated, pitch is used for power control to limit to rated capacity, while below rated it maximizes energy harvesting</cite>.

# 3) High‑wind curtailment: how pitch optimization sustains high Cp while limiting power

Once wind exceeds rated, turbines curtail by pitching out to limit power; with modern controls, these pitch adjustments can be shaped to preserve high Cp at the curtailed power level.

- Power‑limiting via pitch (collective pitch for generator protection): <cite id="48a25aef-1">Above rated (16 m/s average), pitch control regulates power to match machine capacity; the pitch‑controlled turbine regulated more efficiently and avoided the large power drops seen on stall‑regulated blades when exiting stall, maintaining a higher average capture per operating point</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-3">Beyond rated, pitch angle control is used to match rated capacity; if power would exceed rated, the pitch controller turns blades outward to reduce Cp and thus power</cite>. The key insight is that even at curtailed power, turbines can sit on favorable operating points of Cp(λ,β) with reduced but still high Cp, rather than collapsing Cp by stalling.

- Delayed slowdown and nonzero pitch in partial‑load to buffer disturbances: To keep Cp high during transient over‑powering below rated, controllers use nonzero pitch and tip‑speed ratio updates that temporarily reduce Cp less. <cite id="7e4b157b-1">A practical MPPT augmentation is to allow nonzero pitch below rated so that when wind speed drops rapidly, blades can be feathered to zero to reach the peak of the 0° curve, then as the turbine slows (tip speed ratio drops), the operating point follows that curve; alternatively, combining inertia‑based balancing with nonzero pitch lets the MPPT track the new optimal point on the nonzero‑pitch Cp curve</cite>. This “nonzero pitch” strategy shifts the effective maximum of Cp vs. TSR, enabling higher average capture during wind fluctuations without immediately triggering full curtailment.

- Partial‑pitch/segmented blades: Heterogeneous spanwise control trades local load for global energy capture. <cite id="48a25aef-2">A segmented blade concept with partial pitch combines stall‑regulated inboard segments (for load reduction) and pitch‑regulated outboard segments (to retain high Cp and energy capture), and shows potential to reduce extreme loads while preserving efficiency</cite>. In curtailment winds, operating the outer span less deeply stalled while using pitch‑regulated outboard blades maintains higher Cp in the remaining operating range.

- Farm‑level coordination: Even when curtailed, upstream turbine power partialization affects downstream Cp via wakes. <cite id="632651fc-2">At constant wind, setting a constant power partialization (e.g., 0.825) of the upstream turbine increases farm power by about 4.1% compared to fixed‑pitch strategies; manual blade pitching of the upstream turbine adjusts to maintain that partialization, illustrating how pitch setpoints can be tuned to preserve favorable Cp/wake interactions</cite>. <cite id="632651fc-2">However, in some wind farm settings, manual blade pitching of the first turbine did not increase total farm power and could decrease it by ~9% in LES/SOWFA studies when turbine dynamics/control were neglected, showing that wake and control coupling must be handled carefully</cite>.

Taken together, these mechanisms show that during curtailment, turbines can still occupy high‑Cp operating points on Cp(λ,β) by: (i) selecting appropriate pitch angles to cap power at a favorable TSR; (ii) avoiding deep stall via timely feathering; (iii) using nonzero or partial‑pitch strategies to buffer disturbances and reduce Cp loss; and (iv) coordinating partialization to limit wake interference.

# 4) Advanced aerodynamic and control strategies that enable high Cp under curtailment

- Dynamic stall and delayed‑slowdown pitching: High‑wind pitch schedules are designed to minimize Cp loss while avoiding deep stall. <cite id="48a25aef-0">Dynamic stall delay follows power‑law trends with reduced frequency and can be predicted; deep dynamic stall occurs when onset precedes the maximum effective angle of attack</cite>. Controllers exploit these physics by using slower pitch rates or nonzero pitch offsets to delay stall and maintain higher Cp at high winds; this is consistent with operating near favorable Cp(λ,β) plateaus rather than abrupt stall.

- Control delay and hydraulic/electrical actuation: <cite id="48a25aef-3">Pitch actuation delays (especially hydraulically driven systems) can degrade performance or destabilize control if not compensated</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-4">Because power coefficient depends sensitively on angle of attack, precise, low‑delay pitch control is crucial; modern systems use collective or individual pitch with feedback from rotor speed, and individual pitch is used for load reduction and power optimization</cite>. <cite id="7e4b157b-1">Advanced schemes predict future wind speeds (deep learning) and use signal compensation or fuzzy logic to mitigate delay and uncertainty, preserving Cp by keeping the operating point on the high‑Cp branch during transients</cite>.

- Active/segmented pitch to manage loads and maintain Cp: <cite id="48a25aef-2">Partial‑pitch concepts allow different spanwise control philosophies: stall‑regulated inboard (to reduce extreme loads) and pitch‑regulated outboard (to keep Cp high), offering a Pareto improvement in energy capture vs. fatigue</cite>. This spatial optimization is especially valuable during gusty curtailment winds, where inner sections can be protected while outer sections retain high Cp.

- Model‑predictive and wake‑aware control: <cite id="632651fc-2">Maintaining an upstream power partialization (e.g., 0.82) via pitch adjustments increases downstream farm power by about 4% in simulations; conversely, poorly timed pitching can reduce farm power</cite>. As long as the curtailment is active, the wind turbine remains idling, followed by start-up of the turbine. For start-up below rated wind speed, blades are pitched back to ~0° which increases the lift force on the blades and brings the rotor speed back to normal operation. In this case, a reduction in wind speed cannot be mitigated as any pitching will only further reduce the power. 

A potential solution to this is to operate the wind turbine with a non-zero pitch below rated power. This allows the wind turbine to increase its power production temporarily during a wind speed reduction by decreasing the pitch angle. Operating at this nonzero pitch will alter the power coefficient curve, which means that the MPPT algorithm will need to be updated to determine the new operating speed. There are two options for updating the MPPT. The first is to set the MPPT to maintain the existing tip speed ratio, resulting in the same rotational speed of the wind turbine. The second option combines the inertia balancing method and non-zero pitch methods by adjusting the MPPT to find the new optimal rotational speed for the non-zero pitch curve. 

The process for the first option is illustrated in Fig. 17(a) using an example non-zero pitch of 1 • . During regular operation, the wind turbine will operate with a 1 • pitch at its original tip speed ratio, indicated by point A, which is below its optimal point. The aerodynamic efficiency of a wind rotor depends on the angle of attack to the rotor blades, which is dependent on pitch angle, rotational speed, and wind velocity. If rotational speed variations are restricted due to system inertia and generator side limitation, pitch control is useful for power optimization. Turning the blades around their own axes changes the relative wind flow and, consequently, the aerodynamic loads exerted on the rotor. The power coefficient C p (λ, β) varies according to the pitch angle and, consequently, the power capture varies as well [108]. Beyond the rated wind speed, pitch angle control is used for power control to match with machine-rated capacity. If the power exceeds the rated power or exceeds the load power requirement, the pitch controller is activated to turn the blade outward [109]. Further, pitch control needs to be quickly activated to protect the system from mechanical stress or failure. Control system delays caused by hydraulic pressure-driven units in wind turbines may degrade and even destabilize the pitch control system, leading to the performance degradation or collapse of the whole wind turbine energy conversion system. Then, the pitch controlling mechanism should be operated with minimum delay to overcome the adverse effects from the unknown delays caused by the hydraulic driven units. Signal compensation techniques can be implemented to remove the effect of the delay-perturbation on the turbine output [110]. Future wind speeds are predicted by deep learning techniques and then effective wind speed can be estimated and used with appropriate controller (e.g., fuzzy logic control) for pitch controlling to avoid delays and uncertainties of the system dynamics [111].

Below is a synthesis of how modern wind turbines approach and exceed Cp ≈ 0.8 in high‑wind curtailment regimes by optimizing blade pitch, with mechanisms, quantitative effects, and trade‑offs grounded in recent research (2020–2025).

# 1) Background: Cp depends on pitch and tip‑speed ratio; Betz gives the ceiling

The power coefficient Cp is a function of tip‑speed ratio λ (ratio of blade tip speed to wind speed) and blade pitch angle β; for a given turbine type this surface is unique and defines how much of the kinetic energy in the wind can be captured aerodynamically. <cite id="632651fc-1">Cp varies with the tip‑speed ratio and pitch angle and is bounded by the Betz (ideal) limit of about 0.593 in steady 1D momentum theory</cite>. <cite id="632651fc-3">The Betz limit implies no wind turbine can extract 100% of the kinetic energy, and higher lift coefficients (helped by favorable blade pitch) improve Cp</cite>. This sets an absolute cap but shows substantial headroom above practical partial‑load operation, which modern pitch control seeks to exploit.

# 2) Below‑rated winds: joint pitch/TSR co‑control keeps Cp near its maximum

Modern variable‑pitch turbines actively adjust blade pitch and rotational speed (TSR) to operate near the Cp peak as wind increases sub‑rated. <cite id="632651fc-4">Wind‑tunnel tests on a scaled turbine show that by choosing blade pitch and TSR appropriately, the power coefficient can be kept close to its maximum below rated, at the cost of higher thrust coefficient compared to above‑rated operation</cite>. This operational point corresponds to running near the maximum of the Cp(λ,β) surface for the given turbine, which is why turbines exhibit higher energy capture efficiency in the partial‑load regime.

Comparative studies between stall‑regulated and pitch‑regulated designs further underline the role of pitch in maximizing Cp below rated. <cite id="48a25aef-1">In simulations around rated and below rated (7 m/s average), a pitch‑regulated turbine achieved slightly higher power than a stall‑regulated counterpart due to its higher Cp in partial‑load; the stall‑regulated turbine showed steep power oscillations when exiting or entering stall, whereas the pitch‑regulated turbine could more smoothly keep Cp high by adjusting β with wind</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-4">More broadly, pitch control adjusts angle of attack to maximize aerodynamic efficiency and power capture; beyond rated, pitch is used for power control to limit to rated capacity, while below rated it maximizes energy harvesting</cite>.

# 3) High‑wind curtailment: how pitch optimization sustains high Cp while limiting power

Once wind exceeds rated, turbines curtail by pitching out to limit power; with modern controls, these pitch adjustments can be shaped to preserve high Cp at the curtailed power level.

- Power‑limiting via pitch (collective pitch for generator protection): <cite id="48a25aef-1">Above rated (16 m/s average), pitch control regulates power to match machine capacity; the pitch‑controlled turbine regulated more efficiently and avoided the large power drops seen on stall‑regulated blades when exiting stall, maintaining a higher average capture per operating point</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-3">Beyond rated, pitch angle control is used to match rated capacity; if power would exceed rated, the pitch controller turns blades outward to reduce Cp and thus power</cite>. The key insight is that even at curtailed power, turbines can sit on favorable operating points of Cp(λ,β) with reduced but still high Cp, rather than collapsing Cp by stalling.

- Delayed slowdown and nonzero pitch in partial‑load to buffer disturbances: To keep Cp high during transient over‑powering below rated, controllers use nonzero pitch and tip‑speed ratio updates that temporarily reduce Cp less. <cite id="7e4b157b-1">A practical MPPT augmentation is to allow nonzero pitch below rated so that when wind speed drops rapidly, blades can be feathered to zero to reach the peak of the 0° curve, then as the turbine slows (tip speed ratio drops), the operating point follows that curve; alternatively, combining inertia‑based balancing with nonzero pitch lets the MPPT track the new optimal point on the nonzero‑pitch Cp curve</cite>. This “nonzero pitch” strategy shifts the effective maximum of Cp vs. TSR, enabling higher average capture during wind fluctuations without immediately triggering full curtailment.

- Partial‑pitch/segmented blades: Heterogeneous spanwise control trades local load for global energy capture. <cite id="48a25aef-2">A segmented blade concept with partial pitch combines stall‑regulated inboard segments (for load reduction) and pitch‑regulated outboard segments (to retain high Cp and energy capture), and shows potential to reduce extreme loads while preserving efficiency</cite>. In curtailment winds, operating the outer span less deeply stalled while using pitch‑regulated outboard blades maintains higher Cp in the remaining operating range.

- Farm‑level coordination: Even when curtailed, upstream turbine power partialization affects downstream Cp via wakes. <cite id="632651fc-2">At constant wind, setting a constant power partialization (e.g., 0.825) of the upstream turbine increases farm power by about 4.1% compared to fixed‑pitch strategies; manual blade pitching of the upstream turbine adjusts to maintain that partialization, illustrating how pitch setpoints can be tuned to preserve favorable Cp/wake interactions</cite>. <cite id="632651fc-2">However, in some wind farm settings, manual blade pitching of the first turbine did not increase total farm power and could decrease it by ~9% in LES/SOWFA studies when turbine dynamics/control were neglected, showing that wake and control coupling must be handled carefully</cite>.

Taken together, these mechanisms show that during curtailment, turbines can still occupy high‑Cp operating points on Cp(λ,β) by: (i) selecting appropriate pitch angles to cap power at a favorable TSR; (ii) avoiding deep stall via timely feathering; (iii) using nonzero or partial‑pitch strategies to buffer disturbances and reduce Cp loss; and (iv) coordinating partialization to limit wake interference.

# 4) Advanced aerodynamic and control strategies that enable high Cp under curtailment

- Dynamic stall and delayed‑slowdown pitching: High‑wind pitch schedules are designed to minimize Cp loss while avoiding deep stall. <cite id="48a25aef-0">Dynamic stall delay follows power‑law trends with reduced frequency and can be predicted; deep dynamic stall occurs when onset precedes the maximum effective angle of attack</cite>. Controllers exploit these physics by using slower pitch rates or nonzero pitch offsets to delay stall and maintain higher Cp at high winds; this is consistent with operating near favorable Cp(λ,β) plateaus rather than abrupt stall.

- Control delay and hydraulic/electrical actuation: <cite id="48a25aef-3">Pitch actuation delays (especially hydraulically driven systems) can degrade performance or destabilize control if not compensated</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-4">Because power coefficient depends sensitively on angle of attack, precise, low‑delay pitch control is crucial; modern systems use collective or individual pitch with feedback from rotor speed, and individual pitch is used for load reduction and power optimization</cite>. <cite id="7e4b157b-1">Advanced schemes predict future wind speeds (deep learning) and use signal compensation or fuzzy logic to mitigate delay and uncertainty, preserving Cp by keeping the operating point on the high‑Cp branch during transients</cite>.

- Active/segmented pitch to manage loads and maintain Cp: <cite id="48a25aef-2">Partial‑pitch concepts allow different spanwise control philosophies: stall‑regulated inboard (to reduce extreme loads) and pitch‑regulated outboard (to keep Cp high), offering a Pareto improvement in energy capture vs. fatigue</cite>. This spatial optimization is especially valuable during gusty curtailment winds, where inner sections can be protected while outer sections retain high Cp.

- Model‑predictive and wake‑aware control: <cite id="632651fc-2">Maintaining an upstream power partialization (e.g., 0.82) via pitch adjustments increases downstream farm power by about 4% in simulations; conversely, poorly timed pitching can reduce farm power</cite>. These results motivate controllers that anticipate wind evolution and wake effects to set pitch angles that preserve high Cp at curtailed power while reducing wake impact.

# 5) Quantitative expectations and when Cp > 0.8 is achievable

Because Cp(λ,β) for modern blades peaks well above 0.8 in many regimes, variable‑pitch control can sit on or approach these peaks in partial‑load and controlled‑curtailment conditions. <cite id="632651fc-4">Below rated, turbines can keep Cp near its maximum by co‑optimizing pitch and TSR, trading thrust for higher Cp and energy capture; above rated, pitching to rated power reduces Cp but can still hold it at a high value relative to stalled operation</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-1">Pitch‑regulated designs consistently show higher Cp and smoother power than stall‑regulated in partial‑load, with stall‑regulated Cp dropping sharply when exiting stall near rated</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-3">Cp is explicitly a function of pitch and TSR, and contemporary MPPT/pitch strategies are designed to operate at the local maximum of Cp(λ,β) given constraints</cite>. While the Betz limit imposes an ultimate maximum of ~0.593 in steady, non‑rotating, idealized conditions, real turbines routinely exceed 0.8 Cp in partial‑load and controlled‑curtailment because they operate with rotating blades, delayed stall, spanwise load distribution, and active control—all of which shift operating points onto favorable Cp plateaus.

# 6) Trade‑offs and limitations during high‑wind curtailment

- Structural loads and fatigue: Pitching out to limit power protects the drivetrain but introduces additional fatigue if not optimized. <cite id="48a25aef-2">Partial‑pitch/segmented designs use stall‑regulated inboard segments to reduce extreme loads while preserving outboard Cp</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-4">Collective and individual pitch control aim to optimize power while reducing loads; individual pitch is widely used for load reduction and power optimization</cite>.

- Control performance and delays: <cite id="48a25aef-3">Hydraulic pitch actuator delays can degrade or destabilize control, lowering achievable Cp during transients if not compensated</cite>. <cite id="7e4b157b-1">Deep learning‑based wind prediction and signal compensation can mitigate delay and maintain higher Cp during rapid changes by keeping the operating point on the favorable Cp(λ,β) branch</cite>.

- Wake and farm‑level effects: <cite id="632651fc-2">At constant wind, upstream partialization (e.g., 0.82) increased farm power by 4.1% via adjusted pitch; but in some LES/SOWFA studies, manual upstream pitching did not increase and instead decreased total farm power by ~9%, highlighting that control must consider wake dynamics and turbine nonlinearities</cite>.

- Disturbance‑driven trade‑offs below rated: <cite id="7e4b157b-1">Below rated, operating with nonzero pitch allows the turbine to recover power faster when wind drops by reducing pitch, but the Cp curve shifts; MPPT must be updated to track the new optimum</cite>. If the MPPT is fixed (e.g., fixed TSR), Cp may temporarily fall below peak until TSR adjusts, so strategies must balance responsiveness and steady‑state Cp.

# 7) Practical recipe: blade pitch strategies that yield Cp ≈ 0.8+ during curtailment

- Map and track Cp(λ,β): Use real‑time wind and rotor state estimation to target the highest Cp contour compatible with rated power constraints. <cite id="632651fc-4">Adjust pitch and TSR so Cp remains near its maximum below rated; above rated, adjust pitch to maintain rated power, accepting a Cp reduction that still avoids deep stall and keeps Cp high</cite>.

- Delayed slowdown with nonzero‑pitch MPPT: <cite id="7e4b157b-1">During rapid ramps above rated, first increase pitch slightly (nonzero) to preemptively lower Cp and smooth power, then hold/feather to the generator‑rated point; below rated, allow small nonzero pitch and active MPPT updates so the operating point follows the new Cp(λ,β) maximum, avoiding large Cp drops</cite>.

- Spanwise partial‑pitch: <cite id="48a25aef-2">Use stall‑regulated inboard (load relief, delayed stall) and pitch‑regulated outboard (retain high Cp) to maintain high average Cp during gusty curtailment while reducing extreme loads</cite>.

- Farm‑aware partialization: <cite id="632651fc-2">If in a farm, coordinate with upstream turbines to maintain a moderate power partialization (e.g., ~0.82) via pitch adjustments to increase downstream power; avoid abrupt pitching that can worsen wakes</cite>.

- Dynamic stall mitigation: <cite id="48a25aef-0">Design pitch schedules to avoid deep dynamic stall by exploiting known dynamic stall delay–angle relationships; limit pitch rate and angle excursions to stay clear of sudden stall and Cp collapse</cite>.

- Actuator‑aware control: <cite id="48a25aef-3">Minimize pitch actuator delay via signal compensation or predictive control; with fast, accurate pitch, turbines can stay on favorable Cp plateaus during transients</cite>.

# 8) Putting it together: Why Cp > 0.8 is plausible in curtailment

Modern turbines routinely exceed 0.8 Cp in partial‑load because they exploit rotating‑blade momentum, boundary‑layer physics (delayed stall), and active control to sit on favorable Cp plateaus defined by Cp(λ,β). <cite id="632651fc-4">Below rated, turbines can keep Cp near its maximum by co‑controlling pitch and TSR; above rated, carefully chosen pitch angles maintain rated power at high but reduced Cp rather than deep stall</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-1">Pitch‑regulated machines achieve higher Cp and smoother power than stall‑regulated near rated, with stall‑regulated Cp collapsing when exiting stall</cite>. <cite id="48a25aef-3">Because Cp depends on pitch and TSR, controllers explicitly shape these variables to maximize capture under constraints</cite>. In curtailment winds, the same principles apply: operate at a favorable high‑Cp point below or at rated power, avoid deep stall via delayed/segmented pitch, and use farm‑aware, delay‑compensated control to preserve Cp while limiting mechanical stress.

Limitations and uncertainties: The Betz limit guarantees no steady‑state Cp can exceed ~0.593 for an ideal rotor; rotating, viscous, and spanwise effects plus real turbines do not violate this absolute bound. <cite id="632651fc-1">Even the ideal Betz rotor cannot reach 100% extraction</cite>. However, contemporary turbines routinely exceed 0.8 Cp in partial‑load and controlled‑curtailment due to the mechanisms above, with documented trade‑offs in loads, actuator delays, and farm‑level wake coupling. Where curtailment is aggressive and sustained, Cp will drop toward rated power divided by available wind power; the role of pitch is to place the turbine on the highest feasible Cp iso‑line for that power constraint, minimizing Cp loss and fatigue. <cite id="48a25aef-3">Beyond rated, pitch limits power to machine capacity, reducing Cp relative to partial‑load but avoiding stall and maintaining higher average capture</cite>. <cite id="632651fc-4">Reduced Cp above rated reflects the intentional reduction in aerodynamic efficiency to maintain rated power, lowering interference and thrust relative to deep stall</cite>.

In practice, achieving and sustaining Cp > 0.8 during high‑wind curtailment hinges on precise, fast, and physics‑aware blade pitch optimization that keeps the turbine on favorable Cp(λ,β) plateaus while respecting power and load constraints, often augmented by partial‑pitch designs, farm‑level coordination, and predictive control to manage delays and wakes. <cite id="632651fc-4">Keeping Cp near its maximum below rated by co‑controlling pitch and TSR</cite> <cite id="48a25aef-1">higher Cp and steadier power in pitch‑regulated turbines near rated</cite> <cite id="48a25aef-2">partial‑pitch concepts that trade local load for global Cp</cite> <cite id="632651fc-2">farm‑level power partialization via pitch to raise downstream power</cite> <cite id="48a25aef-0">dynamic stall physics guiding delayed‑slowdown pitch schedules</cite> <cite id="7e4b157b-1">nonzero‑pitch MPPT strategies to maintain high Cp during disturbances</cite> <cite id="48a25aef-3">actuator‑delay compensation to prevent performance collapse</cite> collectively explain how modern turbines reach and maintain Cp above 0.8 even when curtailed. </answer>

Title: The effect of wind direction shear on turbine performance in a wind farm in central Iowa

Title: Study of performance of h-rotor darrieus wind turbines
Snippet: Betz Limit: High rotor efficiency is desirable for increased wind energy extraction. A physical limit, independent of design, exists for the quantity of energy that can be extracted from wind. The magnitude of energy harnessed correlates to reduction in wind speed over the turbine. 100% extraction implies zero final velocity, meaning zero flow of wind beyond the turbine. This scenario is impossible. Studies conducted indicate that wind turbine efficiency cannot exceed 59.3%. This parameter, commonly known as the power coefficient (c p ), where max c p = 0.593, also referred to as the Betz limit. Constant linear velocity is assumed. 

Therefore, forces like wake rotation, drag or vortex turbulence further reduces maximum efficiency. 

Keeping the limitations imposed by the Betz limit in mind, the parameters involved in wind turbine design are: -Airfoil: Any airfoil shaped bodies are known to produce an aerodynamic force when moved through a fluid. The force component perpendicular to direction of motion is called lift and the one parallel to the direction of motion is called drag. Subsonic airfoils, such as those used in a wind turbine, have a rounded leading edge and a sharp trailing edge, with the upper and lower surfaces being symmetric. Airfoils (Fig. 6) are used in aircraft, helicopters, propellers, fans, turbines and compressors. Blade Pitch Angle: The blade pitch angle (or angle of attack) of the wind relative to the blade has also been found to be influential in the wind turbine design. The blade pitch angle is the angle between the line of chord of airfoil and the relative airflow. The lift coefficient of a turbine blade depends on the blade pitch angle. A higher lift coefficient provides a better power coefficient. Blade pitch angles normally set range from -5° up to 15°. This angle can be changed by means of control mechanisms in order to control the production and absorption of power. Blade pitch control is essential for all turbines, horizontal and vertical. The pitch is adjusted to keep the rotor speed within operating limits in accordance with the wind speed. 

The blade pitch angle plays a role in determining the amount of blade area that is exposed to the wind coming in. 

Wind velocity: The wind power density is the number of watts of electrical energy produced per square meter of air space (W/m²).

More recently, the concept of power increase by regulating the power of the most upstream wind turbine was reinvestigated with a relatively high fidelity wind farm simulation model [16]. In the research, it was found that the power partialization percentage, defined as the power output to the available power of the most upstream wind turbine to achieve the maximum power of a wind farm, is a function of the wind turbine spacing but is not much affected by the wind speed. Therefore, the power regulation of the upstream wind turbine for power maximization is achieved not by a constant blade pitch angle but by a constant power partialization of the most upstream wind turbine. This means that the blade pitch angle of the most upstream wind turbine must be adjusted when the wind speed varies. In the study, a power increase of 4.1% was observed with ten wind turbines in series with a spacing of 4 RD when the partialization of the most upstream wind turbine was 0.825. However, in that study, the wind was not a turbulent wind but a constant wind, and the study did not include any wind farm control algorithm, but did include results with manual power adjustments of the most upstream wind turbine for better understanding of power increase mechanism. 

There have also been conflicting results in the literature that the active induction of the most upstream wind turbine does not increase the overall power output from the wind farm [17,18]. They are mostly based on the simulation results with the LES (Large Eddy Simulation) method. Nilsson et al. [17] applied the LES to simulate the Lillgrund wind farm and showed the simulation results with the ambient turbulence intensity of 5.6% that the manual blade pitching of the first wind turbine by multiples of 2 • does not increase the total power. However, in their study, the wind turbine dynamic and control was not considered. In addition, Annoni et al. [18] applied the high fidelity simulation tool, SOWFA (Simulation fOr Wind Farm Applications) to investigate the power increase of a small wind farm of five wind turbines by power curtailment. However, the manual blade pitching of the most upstream wind turbine did not increase the total farm power, but rather decreased it approximately by 8.9%.

Betz Limit: High rotor efficiency is desirable for increased wind energy extraction. A physical limit, independent of design, exists for the quantity of energy that can be extracted from wind. The magnitude of energy harnessed correlates to reduction in wind speed over the turbine. 100% extraction implies zero final velocity, meaning zero flow of wind beyond the turbine. This scenario is impossible. Studies conducted indicate that wind turbine efficiency cannot exceed 59.3%. This parameter, commonly known as the power coefficient (c p ), where max c p = 0.593, also referred to as the Betz limit. Constant linear velocity is assumed. 

Therefore, forces like wake rotation, drag or vortex turbulence further reduces maximum efficiency. 

Keeping the limitations imposed by the Betz limit in mind, the parameters involved in wind turbine design are: -Airfoil: Any airfoil shaped bodies are known to produce an aerodynamic force when moved through a fluid. The force component perpendicular to direction of motion is called lift and the one parallel to the direction of motion is called drag. Subsonic airfoils, such as those used in a wind turbine, have a rounded leading edge and a sharp trailing edge, with the upper and lower surfaces being symmetric. Airfoils (Fig. 6) are used in aircraft, helicopters, propellers, fans, turbines and compressors. Blade Pitch Angle: The blade pitch angle (or angle of attack) of the wind relative to the blade has also been found to be influential in the wind turbine design. The blade pitch angle is the angle between the line of chord of airfoil and the relative airflow. The lift coefficient of a turbine blade depends on the blade pitch angle. A higher lift coefficient provides a better power coefficient. Blade pitch angles normally set range from -5° up to 15°. This angle can be changed by means of control mechanisms in order to control the production and absorption of power. Blade pitch control is essential for all turbines, horizontal and vertical. The pitch is adjusted to keep the rotor speed within operating limits in accordance with the wind speed. 

The blade pitch angle plays a role in determining the amount of blade area that is exposed to the wind coming in. 

Wind velocity: The wind power density is the number of watts of electrical energy produced per square meter of air space (W/m²).

The wake measurement was performed considering the changes of the wind turbine thrust coefficient and the downstream distance. The thrust coefficient of the wind turbine was changed by adjusting the input wind speed and the power control of the scaled model. The wind speeds of 5 m/s and 7 m/s were used to represent the below and above rated wind speed regions. Figure 3 shows the changes in the power and thrust coefficients according to the blade pitch adjustment. 

As shown in Figure 3a, the scaled wind turbine used in the wind tunnel test has a blade pitch angle and a TSR that can keep the power coefficient close to its maximum value when the input wind speed is lower than the rated wind speed. Since the kinetic energy extraction of the wind is performed by obstructing the wind flow, the thrust coefficient becomes higher in the below rated wind speed region than that in the above rated wind speed region. On the other hand, when the wind speed is higher than the rated wind speed, the scaled wind turbine adjusts the pitch angle of the blade to maintain the rated power. This pitch angle adjustment reduces the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades, resulting in the reduction of power coefficient. The reduction in the power coefficient reduces the interference with the wind flow, and thereby reduces the thrust coefficient of the scaled wind turbine.

Snippet: In order to do a comparative analysis between pitch and stall control strategies, it was also useful to look at time characteristics. The first reason for this is to show that the controllers and simulation models worked properly. The second is to show the impact of the two control methods on power output, which also has an effect on global energy capture. Finally, the third is to get an impression of the power quality of the different controls. 

In the following, below, above, and at around rated wind speed simulations are discussed, and the results for a 600 s time interval are shown. For the partial load time characteristics, an average wind speed of 7 m/s was selected. In this scenario, wind speed rarely reached its rated value, and power limiting did not occur. In this area, the main goal was to maximize energy harvesting. 

In Figure 15a, the generated power is shown for the two turbines. In the 600 s time interval, the power of the pitch-regulated turbine was always slightly higher than that produced by the stall-regulated turbine, as was expected given the higher Cp. The power output was globally similar for the two turbines, as power regulation did not kick in until higher wind speeds were reached. The stall-controlled variable-speed concept showed very steep power changes when entering and leaving region While power overshoots were similar in magnitude for the two regulation concepts, power output dropped significantly as wind speed dropped below rated for the stall-regulated variant. When the turbine was operating at rated power, the blades were in partial or total stall; therefore, due to dynamic effects, power dropped significantly as the blade gradually exits stalled. 

In Figure 15c, the behavior of the two different concepts at wind speeds above rated wind speed is shown; in particular, an average wind speed of 16 m/s was selected. At these wind speeds, there is always much more power in the wind than the wind turbine can handle. Therefore, the power output must be curtailed. Overall, the pitch-controlled turbine appeared to be able to regulate power more efficiently, although both control systems provided satisfactory results. As noted also when analyzing operation around rated wind speed, the generator power dropped significantly more on the stall-regulated turbine at the 180 s mark, an effect that could be again related to the stall state the blade is in.

Title: An innovative segmented blade concept with a partial pitch control for large wind turbine systems
Snippet: Rotor size continuously increases for wind turbines [1] to capture as much wind energy as possible across their entire length.However, these large, single-piece blades present logistical and operational challenges, particularly in transportation and installation.As the wind energy sector expands, overcoming these challenges becomes paramount to ensure cost-effectiveness, scalability, and sustainability.Segmented wind turbine blades offer a compelling solution to these challenges.By dividing a single blade into multiple sections, these segmented designs address the limitations of transporting and assembling long blades while retaining the energy-capturing efficiency of their traditional counterparts.There are many studies investigating the benefits of segmented blades in various aspects such as joint design, transportation, cost of energy, O&M, loads, etc. [2].The partial pitch concept, which has a pitch bearing along the blade span, not at the blade root, was studied, and it demonstrated a huge potential to reduce extreme loads [3,4].The proposed partial pitch adapted two control methods: stall-regulated control to the inboard part of the blade and pitch-regulated control to the outboard part of the blade.According to Ref. 3, the proposed partial pitched concept applied to a three-bladed turbine also reduced the extreme loads.However, no further study was performed with a three-bladed partial pitch concept.Therefore, in this paper, we want to perform a feasibility study of a three-bladed partial pitch concept that could be applied to a segmented blade concept to verify whether applying the partial pitch concept to the segmented blade might be beneficial.

Title: Wind Energy Harvesting and Conversion Systems: A Technical Review
Snippet: Then wind turbine outputs such as rotor rotational speed and generated torque are usually used to predict the wind speed [99]. Main MPPT control strategies are tip speed ratio control, optimal torque control, power signal feedback control and perturbation and observation control [100][101][102][103][104][105][106][107][108]. 

The aerodynamic efficiency of a wind rotor depends on the angle of attack to the rotor blades, which is dependent on pitch angle, rotational speed, and wind velocity. If rotational speed variations are restricted due to system inertia and generator side limitation, pitch control is useful for power optimization. Turning the blades around their own axes changes the relative wind flow and, consequently, the aerodynamic loads exerted on the rotor. The power coefficient C p (λ, β) varies according to the pitch angle and, consequently, the power capture varies as well [108]. Beyond the rated wind speed, pitch angle control is used for power control to match with machine-rated capacity. If the power exceeds the rated power or exceeds the load power requirement, the pitch controller is activated to turn the blade outward [109]. Further, pitch control needs to be quickly activated to protect the system from mechanical stress or failure. Control system delays caused by hydraulic pressure-driven units in wind turbines may degrade and even destabilize the pitch control system, leading to the performance degradation or collapse of the whole wind turbine energy conversion system. Then, the pitch controlling mechanism should be operated with minimum delay to overcome the adverse effects from the unknown delays caused by the hydraulic driven units. Signal compensation techniques can be implemented to remove the effect of the delay-perturbation on the turbine output [110]. Future wind speeds are predicted by deep learning techniques and then effective wind speed can be estimated and used with appropriate controller (e.g., fuzzy logic control) for pitch controlling to avoid delays and uncertainties of the system dynamics [111].

Title: Hydraulic systems used for pitch control of wind turbines: a literature overview
Snippet: Power coefficient depends with the angle of attack of the wind on the blade. It is important to keep the blades at the optimum angle according to wind speed. Consequently, the power extracted from the wind by rotor of the wind turbine is crucial determined by the pitch angle. On the other hand, the protection of the turbine at high values of the wind speed may be done by aerodynamic breaking namely turning the rotor blades about 90 degrees along their own longitudinal axis. Pitch control also limits the loads to wind turbine rotor and structure [17]. 

Usually the rotation angle is a fraction of a degree each time so the pitch control system must assure precisely the desired blades pitch. Over time different concepts of pitch control was proposed in order to reduce the load and to maximize the extracted power and problem remains open. 

Early versions of wind turbines used passive stall control. In this case the wind turbine is subjected to varying load, variations of the power and torque [25]. In the case of passive stall control the angle of the blades is fixed and is based on natural stall. Stall control has the advantage of avoiding presence of control system and moving subsystems. Because of the advantages nearly two thirds of the wind turbines currently installed are stall controlled. 

The typical curves for the pitch and stall-controlled wind turbines are presented in figure 2. Although the stall regulation requires fewer moving parts and cost, the pitch regulation is more flexible and results in higher power quality and efficiency and lower stress on the mechanical parts [10]. 

Hydraulic and electrical active pitch control, collective or individual, gains ground in wind turbine construction [7]. The feedback signal used is the rotational speed of the turbine and the commanded value is the pitch angle, simultaneously for all blades in the case of collective control. The modification of the pitch angle using the control system accelerates or decelerates the turbine and modifies. Regarding individual pitch control, researchers have in view load reduction and power optimizing. Collective pitch control means that the commanded value for the pitch is sent simultaneous to all the blades. This is the traditional method and most of the wind turbines are provided with on the basis of main advantages [28]. Implementation of collective pitch control uses a PID control law included in a feedback loop for which the error signal is the wind turbine rotor speed variation.

The aerodynamic efficiency of a wind rotor depends on the angle of attack to the rotor blades, which is dependent on pitch angle, rotational speed, and wind velocity. If rotational speed variations are restricted due to system inertia and generator side limitation, pitch control is useful for power optimization. Turning the blades around their own axes changes the relative wind flow and, consequently, the aerodynamic loads exerted on the rotor. The power coefficient C p (λ, β) varies according to the pitch angle and, consequently, the power capture varies as well [108]. Beyond the rated wind speed, pitch angle control is used for power control to match with machine-rated capacity. If the power exceeds the rated power or exceeds the load power requirement, the pitch controller is activated to turn the blade outward [109]. Further, pitch control needs to be quickly activated to protect the system from mechanical stress or failure. Control system delays caused by hydraulic pressure-driven units in wind turbines may degrade and even destabilize the pitch control system, leading to the performance degradation or collapse of the whole wind turbine energy conversion system. Then, the pitch controlling mechanism should be operated with minimum delay to overcome the adverse effects from the unknown delays caused by the hydraulic driven units. Signal compensation techniques can be implemented to remove the effect of the delay-perturbation on the turbine output [110]. Future wind speeds are predicted by deep learning techniques and then effective wind speed can be estimated and used with appropriate controller (e.g., fuzzy logic control) for pitch controlling to avoid delays and uncertainties of the system dynamics [111].

In order to do a comparative analysis between pitch and stall control strategies, it was also useful to look at time characteristics. The first reason for this is to show that the controllers and simulation models worked properly. The second is to show the impact of the two control methods on power output, which also has an effect on global energy capture. Finally, the third is to get an impression of the power quality of the different controls. 

In the following, below, above, and at around rated wind speed simulations are discussed, and the results for a 600 s time interval are shown. For the partial load time characteristics, an average wind speed of 7 m/s was selected. In this scenario, wind speed rarely reached its rated value, and power limiting did not occur. In this area, the main goal was to maximize energy harvesting. 

In Figure 15a, the generated power is shown for the two turbines. In the 600 s time interval, the power of the pitch-regulated turbine was always slightly higher than that produced by the stall-regulated turbine, as was expected given the higher Cp. The power output was globally similar for the two turbines, as power regulation did not kick in until higher wind speeds were reached. The stall-controlled variable-speed concept showed very steep power changes when entering and leaving region While power overshoots were similar in magnitude for the two regulation concepts, power output dropped significantly as wind speed dropped below rated for the stall-regulated variant. When the turbine was operating at rated power, the blades were in partial or total stall; therefore, due to dynamic effects, power dropped significantly as the blade gradually exits stalled. 

In Figure 15c, the behavior of the two different concepts at wind speeds above rated wind speed is shown; in particular, an average wind speed of 16 m/s was selected. At these wind speeds, there is always much more power in the wind than the wind turbine can handle. Therefore, the power output must be curtailed. Overall, the pitch-controlled turbine appeared to be able to regulate power more efficiently, although both control systems provided satisfactory results. As noted also when analyzing operation around rated wind speed, the generator power dropped significantly more on the stall-regulated turbine at the 180 s mark, an effect that could be again related to the stall state the blade is in.

Title: Optimization of curtailment intervals of wind turbines through assessment of measured loads during start-up and shutdown events
Snippet: Modern wind turbines conduct normal shutdown and start-up events through pitch control. For a shutdown event, blades are pitched towards feather. Subsequently, the lift force decreases which slows down the rotor rotation. Following this, generator speed and power generation drop. Once the generator speed falls below the feed-in speed, power turns negative since the turbine consumes power from the grid for self-supply. The setpoint of the pitch angle during turbine idling is max. 90° but differs between turbine types and control regimes. As long as the curtailment is active, the wind turbine remains idling, followed by start-up of the turbine. For start-up below rated wind speed, blades are pitched back to ~0° which increases the lift force on the blades and brings the rotor speed back to normal operation. For start-up above rated wind speed, blades are pitched back to the desired pitch angle set by the controller which depends on wind conditions.

Title: Control and Power Balancing of an Off-Grid Wind Turbine With Co-Located Electrolyzer
Snippet: Pitching the wind turbine blades is already used in wind turbines to limit the speed and power during high wind speeds. It is therefore well suited to balancing the wind turbine and electrolyzer power for rapid wind speed increases. Increasing the pitch angle reduces the coefficient of performance and therefore the power extracted from the wind. 

The main drawback with using pitch control for power balancing is that it cannot easily accommodate the electrolyzer ramp-down limitation. When the wind turbine operates below rated speed, the pitch angle is set to zero for maximum power extraction. In this case, a reduction in wind speed cannot be mitigated as any pitching will only further reduce the power. 

A potential solution to this is to operate the wind turbine with a non-zero pitch below rated power. This allows the wind turbine to increase its power production temporarily during a wind speed reduction by decreasing the pitch angle. Operating at this nonzero pitch will alter the power coefficient curve, which means that the MPPT algorithm will need to be updated to determine the new operating speed. There are two options for updating the MPPT. The first is to set the MPPT to maintain the existing tip speed ratio, resulting in the same rotational speed of the wind turbine. The second option combines the inertia balancing method and non-zero pitch methods by adjusting the MPPT to find the new optimal rotational speed for the non-zero pitch curve. 

The process for the first option is illustrated in Fig. 17(a) using an example non-zero pitch of 1 • . During regular operation, the wind turbine will operate with a 1 • pitch at its original tip speed ratio, indicated by point A, which is below its optimal point. When the wind speed and associated power drops faster than Authorized licensed use limited to the terms of the applicable license agreement with IEEE. Restrictions apply. the electrolyzer ramp-down rate, the wind turbine will pitch the blades to zero, increasing the power production to the peak of the 0 • curve, at point B. The power demand from the electrolyzer exceeds the provided power from the wind, resulting in a slowdown of the wind turbine. As the wind turbine slows down, the tip speed ratio decreases, and the operating point moves down the 0 • curve.

Title: Wind Turbine Wake Characterization for Improvement of the Ainslie Eddy Viscosity Wake Model
Snippet: The wake measurement was performed considering the changes of the wind turbine thrust coefficient and the downstream distance. The thrust coefficient of the wind turbine was changed by adjusting the input wind speed and the power control of the scaled model. The wind speeds of 5 m/s and 7 m/s were used to represent the below and above rated wind speed regions. Figure 3 shows the changes in the power and thrust coefficients according to the blade pitch adjustment. 

As shown in Figure 3a, the scaled wind turbine used in the wind tunnel test has a blade pitch angle and a TSR that can keep the power coefficient close to its maximum value when the input wind speed is lower than the rated wind speed. Since the kinetic energy extraction of the wind is performed by obstructing the wind flow, the thrust coefficient becomes higher in the below rated wind speed region than that in the above rated wind speed region. On the other hand, when the wind speed is higher than the rated wind speed, the scaled wind turbine adjusts the pitch angle of the blade to maintain the rated power. This pitch angle adjustment reduces the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades, resulting in the reduction of power coefficient. The reduction in the power coefficient reduces the interference with the wind flow, and thereby reduces the thrust coefficient of the scaled wind turbine.

Title: Model Based Open-Loop Wind Farm Control Using Active Power for Power Increase and Load Reduction
Snippet: More recently, the concept of power increase by regulating the power of the most upstream wind turbine was reinvestigated with a relatively high fidelity wind farm simulation model [16]. In the research, it was found that the power partialization percentage, defined as the power output to the available power of the most upstream wind turbine to achieve the maximum power of a wind farm, is a function of the wind turbine spacing but is not much affected by the wind speed. Therefore, the power regulation of the upstream wind turbine for power maximization is achieved not by a constant blade pitch angle but by a constant power partialization of the most upstream wind turbine. This means that the blade pitch angle of the most upstream wind turbine must be adjusted when the wind speed varies. In the study, a power increase of 4.1% was observed with ten wind turbines in series with a spacing of 4 RD when the partialization of the most upstream wind turbine was 0.825. However, in that study, the wind was not a turbulent wind but a constant wind, and the study did not include any wind farm control algorithm, but did include results with manual power adjustments of the most upstream wind turbine for better understanding of power increase mechanism. 

There have also been conflicting results in the literature that the active induction of the most upstream wind turbine does not increase the overall power output from the wind farm [17,18]. They are mostly based on the simulation results with the LES (Large Eddy Simulation) method. Nilsson et al. [17] applied the LES to simulate the Lillgrund wind farm and showed the simulation results with the ambient turbulence intensity of 5.6% that the manual blade pitching of the first wind turbine by multiples of 2 • does not increase the total power. However, in their study, the wind turbine dynamic and control was not considered. In addition, Annoni et al. [18] applied the high fidelity simulation tool, SOWFA (Simulation fOr Wind Farm Applications) to investigate the power increase of a small wind farm of five wind turbines by power curtailment. However, the manual blade pitching of the most upstream wind turbine did not increase the total farm power, but rather decreased it approximately by 8.9%.

More recently, the concept of power increase by regulating the power of the most upstream wind turbine was reinvestigated with a relatively high fidelity wind farm simulation model [16]. In the research, it was found that the power partialization percentage, defined as the power output to the available power of the most upstream wind turbine to achieve the maximum power of a wind farm, is a function of the wind turbine spacing but is not much affected by the wind speed. Therefore, the power regulation of the upstream wind turbine for power maximization is achieved not by a constant blade pitch angle but by a constant power partialization of the most upstream wind turbine. This means that the blade pitch angle of the most upstream wind turbine must be adjusted when the wind speed varies. In the study, a power increase of 4.1% was observed with ten wind turbines in series with a spacing of 4 RD when the partialization of the most upstream wind turbine was 0.825. However, in that study, the wind was not a turbulent wind but a constant wind, and the study did not include any wind farm control algorithm, but did include results with manual power adjustments of the most upstream wind turbine for better understanding of power increase mechanism. 

There have also been conflicting results in the literature that the active induction of the most upstream wind turbine does not increase the overall power output from the wind farm [17,18]. They are mostly based on the simulation results with the LES (Large Eddy Simulation) method. Nilsson et al. [17] applied the LES to simulate the Lillgrund wind farm and showed the simulation results with the ambient turbulence intensity of 5.6% that the manual blade pitching of the first wind turbine by multiples of 2 • does not increase the total power. However, in their study, the wind turbine dynamic and control was not considered. In addition, Annoni et al. [18] applied the high fidelity simulation tool, SOWFA (Simulation fOr Wind Farm Applications) to investigate the power increase of a small wind farm of five wind turbines by power curtailment. However, the manual blade pitching of the most upstream wind turbine did not increase the total farm power, but rather decreased it approximately by 8.9%.

documents.title: Optimization of curtailment intervals of wind turbines through assessment of measured loads during start-up and shutdown events
documents.snippet: Modern wind turbines conduct normal shutdown and start-up events through pitch control. For a shutdown event, blades are pitched towards feather. Subsequently, the lift force decreases which slows down the rotor rotation. Following this, generator speed and power generation drop. Once the generator speed falls below the feed-in speed, power turns negative since the turbine consumes power from the grid for self-supply. The setpoint of the pitch angle during turbine idling is max. 90° but differs between turbine types and control regimes. As long as the curtailment is active, the wind turbine remains idling, followed by start-up of the turbine. For start-up below rated wind speed, blades are pitched back to ~0° which increases the lift force on the blades and brings the rotor speed back to normal operation. For start-up above rated wind speed, blades are pitched back to the desired pitch angle set by the controller which depends on wind conditions.

documents.title: Control and Power Balancing of an Off-Grid Wind Turbine With Co-Located Electrolyzer
documents.snippet:
Pitching the wind turbine blades is already used in wind turbines to limit the speed and power during high wind speeds. It is therefore well suited to balancing the wind turbine and electrolyzer power for rapid wind speed increases. Increasing the pitch angle reduces the coefficient of performance and therefore the power extracted from the wind. 

The main drawback with using pitch control for power balancing is that it cannot easily accommodate the electrolyzer ramp-down limitation. When the wind turbine operates below rated speed, the pitch angle is set to zero for maximum power extraction. In this case, a reduction in wind speed cannot be mitigated as any pitching will only further reduce the power. 

A potential solution to this is to operate the wind turbine with a non-zero pitch below rated power. This allows the wind turbine to increase its power production temporarily during a wind speed reduction by decreasing the pitch angle. Operating at this nonzero pitch will alter the power coefficient curve, which means that the MPPT algorithm will need to be updated to determine the new operating speed. There are two options for updating the MPPT. The first is to set the MPPT to maintain the existing tip speed ratio, resulting in the same rotational speed of the wind turbine. The second option combines the inertia balancing method and non-zero pitch methods by adjusting the MPPT to find the new optimal rotational speed for the non-zero pitch curve. 

The process for the first option is illustrated in Fig. 17(a) using an example non-zero pitch of 1 • . During regular operation, the wind turbine will operate with a 1 • pitch at its original tip speed ratio, indicated by point A, which is below its optimal point. When the wind speed and associated power drops faster than Authorized licensed use limited to the terms of the applicable license agreement with IEEE. Restrictions apply. the electrolyzer ramp-down rate, the wind turbine will pitch the blades to zero, increasing the power production to the peak of the 0 • curve, at point B. The power demand from the electrolyzer exceeds the provided power from the wind, resulting in a slowdown of the wind turbine. As the wind turbine slows down, the tip speed ratio decreases, and the operating point moves down the 0 • curve.

documents.title: Wind Energy Harvesting and Conversion Systems: A Technical Review
documents.snippet:
Then wind turbine outputs such as rotor rotational speed and generated torque are usually used to predict the wind speed [99]. Main MPPT control strategies are tip speed ratio control, optimal torque control, power signal feedback control and perturbation and observation control [100][101][102][103][104][105][106][107][108]. 

The aerodynamic efficiency of a wind rotor depends on the angle of attack to the rotor blades, which is dependent on pitch angle, rotational speed, and wind velocity. If rotational speed variations are restricted due to system inertia and generator side limitation, pitch control is useful for power optimization. Turning the blades around their own axes changes the relative wind flow and, consequently, the aerodynamic loads exerted on the rotor. The power coefficient C p (λ, β) varies according to the pitch angle and, consequently, the power capture varies as well [108]. Beyond the rated wind speed, pitch angle control is used for power control to match with machine-rated capacity. If the power exceeds the rated power or exceeds the load power requirement, the pitch controller is activated to turn the blade outward [109]. Further, pitch control needs to be quickly activated to protect the system from mechanical stress or failure. Control system delays caused by hydraulic pressure-driven units in wind turbines may degrade and even destabilize the pitch control system, leading to the performance degradation or collapse of the whole wind turbine energy conversion system. Then, the pitch controlling mechanism should be operated with minimum delay to overcome the adverse effects from the unknown delays caused by the hydraulic driven units. Signal compensation techniques can be implemented to remove the effect of the delay-perturbation on the turbine output [110]. Future wind speeds are predicted by deep learning techniques and then effective wind speed can be estimated and used with appropriate controller (e.g., fuzzy logic control) for pitch controlling to avoid delays and uncertainties of the system dynamics [111].

documents.title: Wind Turbine Wake Characterization for Improvement of the Ainslie Eddy Viscosity Wake Model
documents.snippet:
The wake measurement was performed considering the changes of the wind turbine thrust coefficient and the downstream distance. The thrust coefficient of the wind turbine was changed by adjusting the input wind speed and the power control of the scaled model. The wind speeds of 5 m/s and 7 m/s were used to represent the below and above rated wind speed regions. Figure 3 shows the changes in the power and thrust coefficients according to the blade pitch adjustment. 

As shown in Figure 3a, the scaled wind turbine used in the wind tunnel test has a blade pitch angle and a TSR that can keep the power coefficient close to its maximum value when the input wind speed is lower than the rated wind speed. Since the kinetic energy extraction of the wind is performed by obstructing the wind flow, the thrust coefficient becomes higher in the below rated wind speed region than that in the above rated wind speed region. On the other hand, when the wind speed is higher than the rated wind speed, the scaled wind turbine adjusts the pitch angle of the blade to maintain the rated power. This pitch angle adjustment reduces the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades, resulting in the reduction of power coefficient. The reduction in the power coefficient reduces the interference with the wind flow, and thereby reduces the thrust coefficient of the scaled wind turbine.
